Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first part of the question may I say how much I regret certain statements on this very important question made by some CBC reporters which seem to have been made without checking with us. The shelf life of the influenza vaccine from laboratory tests has been estimated to be about 12 months. Based on experience in the United States with type A influenza strains, it is believed that immunity after vaccination could last up to three years in a significant portion of the population, provided there were no changes in the antigenic makeup of the virus.

Deliveries have not yet been received. It is hoped that the vaccine will be available for the coming 'flu season. speechtext: This is a bill to amend the Combines Investigation Act to provide for the standardization of warranties and to define the minimum provisions thereof. When the consumer reads the warranty's fine print, he discovers that the document is so full of exceptions and qualifications that it is almost useless. This bill will correct these anomalies.
Motion agreed to, bill read the first time and ordered to be printed.

speechtext: With reference to the answer to Question No. 4,109 of the First Session of the 30th Parliament, referring in part to efforts to establish a National Terminology Bank by the Secretary of State in conjunction with the University of Montreal, what (a) is a description of this proposed facility and its purpose (b) is the estimated cost (c) are the reasons for its creation (d) are the number of public service personnel to be involved and their estimated annual salaries?

subsubtopic: NATIONAL TERMINOLOGY BANK
speechtext:
(a) The terminology bank will involve the computerized collection of terminology in use or likely to be used by government services. Each term in the bank will be defined or used in context, and access to the terms will be provided by various parameters or combinations of parameters (e.g.: area of usage, source, reliability, geographic origin), in each language for which the term exists. The terminology will be multilingual to the extent that the government requires terms in non-official languages. The bank will be instrumental in centralizing available terminological information, particularly for the purposes of translation within government departments, and invaluable in meeting the requirements of language standardization in the Public Ser-

1.	Has the government given any consideration to studying whether the Public Service Commission, by its own volition or by legislative restraint, operates competitions in Atlantic Canada which cannot be entered by members of the Canadian Armed Forces who, while posted elsewhere, formerly resided in Atlantic Canada and wish to return to employment in the Public Service in Atlantic Canada and, if not, for what reason?
2.	What is the government's considered view of the effect such a policy might have on Atlantic Canada's efforts to prevent the permanent exodus of talented individuals?

I am informed by the Public Service Commission as follows: 1. The answer to this question is negative because of the following: The Public Service Commission is restrained by legislation in determining who is eligible to compete in competitions. When selection is to be made from among persons employed in the Public Service, the candidates' eligibility for appointment, known as the area of competition, is determined by the positions in which they are employed. When selection is to be made from among applicants from outside the Public Service, eligibility for appointment is defined in terms of the area in which candidates must reside. The Public Service Commission has however, established a policy that recognizes the special circumstances confronting retiring members of the Canadian Armed Forces seeking employment in the Public Service. The policy provides, that, where the area of competition includes residency requirements, members of the Canadian Armed Forces may claim entitlement to compete on the basis either of the locality where they are stationed or where their immediate families reside. In its opinion, the Commission can offer no greater flexibility in its policies for the determination of area of competition without both exceeding the provisions of the Public Service Employment Act and being discriminatory in favour of the Canadian Armed Forces.
2. Having no data on the incidence of the return of members of the Armed Forces to Atlantic Canada upon leaving the Forces, the Commission can express no views in response to this question.

subsubtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
1.	Is posted mail sent to particular locations for sorting and, if so, what mail is sorted in Montreal from areas other than the Province of Quebec?
2.	Has any mail, sent for sorting in Montreal, been redirected to Saint John, New Brunswick and, if so, in what quantities and for what reasons?

subsubtopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
1. Mail is first sorted at the office at which it is posted. The practice is to send mail matter directly from the office of origin to the office of address. Where, because of lack of volume for a particular office of address, this is not possible, mail is sent to an intermediate office for further sorting. The intermediate office most used by post offices in Canada for the province of Quebec is Montreal, and therefore mail originating all across Canada is sent to Montreal to be forwarded to its final destination in the province of Quebec. In addition to this, Montreal is one of the main terminating points for air mail from overseas destinations, and mail addressed to many points in Canada is sent to Montreal by foreign administrations for transmission to points in Canada.
2. No, except that mail originating in Quebec province addressed to smaller places in New Brunswick, which had been sent to Montreal by smaller post offices in the province of Quebec because there was not enough to make a direct despatch, may have been sent to Saint John for transmission to points in New Brunswick.

The House resumed, from Monday, November 1, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott that Bill C-16, to provide for the protection of borrowers and depositors, to regulate interest on judgment debts, to repeal the Interest Act, the Pawnbrokers Act and the Small Loans Act and to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I said last night on this bill, we rejoice in its presentation though I regret, naturally, that the government as a federal institution, should have waited so long before bringing forward this very important piece of legislation.
I also said that, Canadian personal debts having increased considerably in the last ten years, to the extent of now representing almost 22 per cent of their disposable income, it is that much more imperative for the government to present those amendments today. What makes this bill interesting is the fact that, once again, its scope is extremely vast. It encompasses all transactions that can concern Canadians individually, and small businesses in the field of borrowing, as well as all Canadians with regard to managing their savings.
In addition, it increases the quality and quantity of credit information; it eliminates useless complications in the field of credit, it reduces to a large extent the possibility of excessively high rates of interest on credit, for we are introducing here the concept of unwarranted interest rates by making it incumbent upon the lender to prove that the interest he charges the borrower is in fact a just rate considering the risks involved and the cost of the capital. We are also introducing the concept of a criminal rate in that when the lender's rates clearly exceed justifiable ones, the guilty is liable not only to a fine but also to imprisonment.
678

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
Through this bill, we are also able to rationalize the federal legislation and to establish a strict and uniform legislation regarding consumer credit regulations. Yesterday I expressed some doubts about the constitutional character of this bill and I asked the minister to dispel the fears expressed on this matter by some hon. members, particularly by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert). I think a good way to understand the significance and timeliness of this bill would be to give examples of some conditions we have today in Canada and against which there is absolutely no legal protection. For example, most depositors are not really paid interest on their deposits as the computation of interest on deposits is made half-yearly on the lowest balance in their accounts. Consequently, tens and tens of millions of dollars are thus lost because that procedure is precisely opposite to that used by lenders when they compute the rate of interest for borrowers.
Another example. If we think that our solvency will allow us to get lower monthly interest rate levied on our loan, we are no doubt deluding ourselves. Yesterday, 1 referred to the same individual who applies to the same institution but does not use the same system to borrow money, either a bank credit card, a negotiated loan or a term loan. He will be granted a loan with different interest rates.
It is the same for advertising. The various financial institutions are allowed to announce a certain interest rate on savings when in fact the interest rate is much lower. For example, it is quite possible to announce that an interest rate of 8 per cent will be paid on deposits when indeed it will be 5 or 5.2 per cent while this reference to 8 per cent in an advertisement is legal. At the same time, interest charged to borrowers is often greater than the interest rate announced. This is another area that will be settled through this bill. As I said yesterday, this legislation will provide us with the necessary means to pursue lenders who charge usurious rates: 300, 400, 500, and sometimes as much as 2,000 per cent. I recalled yesterday that according to the best information we have, police forces feel that loans at usurious rates now constitute the second financing source of organized crime, of the underworld, the mafia.
This piece of legislation will also provide police force with a toot to dry up this very important source of financing organized crime in Canada. These are but a few aspects of this bill and I hope that through committee deliberations all hon. members of this House will entertain the same spirit to improve the bill where they think certain aspects deserve to be improved. I would like some explanations on the possibility of calculating interest rates on a daily basis. I would like to know to what extent this responsibility will be feasible under this bill for small lending companies. Would not calculation on a monthly basis be more realistic? It is up to the minister to supply us with figures. The responsibility should not be too costly for lending companies or, conversely, it would frustrate borrowers of very important sums. But, on first approach, it seems to me that generally, for relatively small loans, calculation on a monthly rather than on a daily basis would be adequate.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad this bill has been introduced and I hope it will not be the object of a filibuster similar to that which marred the introduction of the first bill on competition. I think that Canadians generally agree that we have not really done much up to now to protect them in this area. In my opinion that is why this bill, which meets a pressing need on the part of Canadian consumers, arrives in the nick of time.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to participate in the debate on Bill C-16, the borrowers and depositors protection act. I acknowledge that this is an important bill and wonder, with respect to a bill of this magnitude, of such far-reaching effect on the social scene and to the financial community of Canada, why the opposition was given only 120 hours between first reading and second reading to prepare itself for debate. We are left in this position: as debate proceeds, research papers 60 and 70 pages thick are arriving. We are supposed to know the contents of those papers to make sure the people of Canada are getting improved legislation in this area. I ask, what is the rush with this bill? It is important legislation.
I am greatly concerned because the bill relies heavily on regulation. Throughout the bill there are references to regulations, which indicates to me that the homework done by its drafters was somewhat inadequate. I noticed that in his introductory remarks the minister complimented his staff. I congratulate him for acknowledging the hard work they have done and the extensive communications his departmental people entered into with other departments of government. But having read the bill two or three times, together with some of the available research material, I am led to conclude that there has been little consultation with the business community on some of the spin-off effects of the bill in the private sector. I ask, why would a new, ambitious, obviously smart, somewhat brilliant and youthful minister rush in-

speechtext:
He is a pretty bright guy. Why would this minister rush into a portfolio from which a wise, respected old owl saw fit to rush out? In my opinion, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has not brought forward much successful legislation, its legislative record is not good. Nor has it been able properly to enforce existing consumer legislation. Perhaps I can say that the only reason I am in the House today is my astonishment with a former minister of that department who was unable to understand that there can be two points of view.
I am deeply concerned about some aspects of this bill, and completely sympathetic to others. I wonder why the bill was not given the benefit of further consultation with other interested parties affected by it, so that we could look beyond the purview of political opportunism and not get caught in the fly-paper, which is what I feel will happen. The political anxiety to serve the consumer will create secondary effects
November 2, 1976

which, with more preparation and more listening to a wider audience, could have been prevented.
Let me now list those parts of the bill of which I fully approve. I compliment the government on requiring full and complete disclosure of all loan costs. 1 think this step is past due. Also, credit charges are to be calculated on a net principal sum, which means the net money the borrower actually receives. This, too, is a step in the right direction. The bill deals with control of advertising, which 1 agree is important. We agree with some provisions of the bill which apply to some lenders. The bill contains provisions with respect to the prepayment of fixed rate mortgages. I agree with the implementation of this aspect of the bill in a market of rising interest rates. However, I do not think provisions concerning variable mortgage rates have been well thought out by drafters of the bill and I shall deal with that point as I proceed with my remarks.
I believe that the maintenance of requisite records is necessary if the bill is to be meaningful, but wonder how many man-years of employment will be created in any new bureaucracy set up to deal with such matters. As the minister said in his press release, the bill places great emphasis on the curtailment of loan-sharking. 1 agree that coercive acts, threats or certain misrepresentations in this regard on the part of lenders should be brought under the Criminal Code. There is not any member on my side of the House who does not recognize that these are important aspects of the bill, and I hope that other parts of the bill can be improved as we study it. We hope that eventually good legislation will be placed in the statute books. However, I would not want to see the very positive aspects of the bill disrupted or discouraged, with unforeseen hazards and damaging repercussions to the business sector of this country. One thing that has happened to this country since 1972 and that we are paying for today is disruption of the decision-making base. We have a tendency to legislate in order to curb and correct abuses. This is good. However, let us make sure that we do not add more confusion to the productive sector of the economy which is having great trouble today.
I have said before in this House that one of the problems we are having in the west with this type of legislation and legislation that relies extensively on regulation is that we do not trust the federal scene anymore. That is why I have offered some comments about my concern as to why this bill is being rushed into the House and why it is being put before the health and welfare committee instead of the finance committee. 1 repeat my regret that I have not had an opportunity to become fully researched and aware of all the implications of this legislation.
Having seen how some of the committees have been manipulated and handled in the past, 1 have to wonder how extensive a hearing the bill will receive in committee, and to what kind of manipulation it will be subjected by the steering committee and the standing committee it goes before. Will the banks, trust companies, mortgage companies and financial institutions in this country be encouraged to present briefs so that we
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors can minimize the spin-off, detrimental effects that some of these measures might have within the country? Like some of my colleagues, I have very real concern about the effectiveness of the committee system as it is presently being managed by some ministers.
In the research leading to this bill there have been extensive briefs from consumer organizations. As far as my files are concerned, there is an absolute dirth with regard to briefs from the industry which have been the subject of this legislation; this is a void of which industries, if they read Hansard, should be aware. When the bill comes back into this House at report stage, 1 hope that suddenly many aspects of the Canadian community do not only then wake up to the fact that very serious legislation is being imposed upon them. I would like to see full input at the committee stage of this bill. I hope the minister will encourage that type of activity in the steering committee proceedings and in the committee proceedings.
There are some spin-offs that will be quite serious in the Canadian community in the attempts to bring about legislation that will protect the low income borrower. I hope these spinoffs can be prevented and the bill can be kept within its original intent and principle. 1 wonder if the authors of the bill and the minister are fully aware of the changes that will be forced upon the community.
In the time allowed me to participate in this debate I will try to bring out one or two areas of real concern. Is the bill going to dry up funds and aggravate, rather than alleviate, the situation for the marginal borrower? I hope that in committee there will be full exploration of that aspect and that there will be incentives left or placed within the industry to serve the needs of the low income borrower. To what extent will the bill centralize the lending power of the industry into federal hands? Do the provinces really agree with this centralization? Has the minister had full discourse with his counterparts on the provincial scene? According to a paper that I was able to have typed up just yesterday, there are extensive legal debates ahead for this piece of legislation as it is presently drafted. I have been talking to people in two provincial departments. I find that they are going to resist any centralization of these powers or interference with powers that they are already enjoying in legislation that they implemented well in advance of this bill being presented to the House of Commons.
Is the minister fully aware of who will be the real beneficiaries as a result of this legislation? The reason 1 ask a question of that nature is that we jumped into the situation where we could offer the Canadian taxpayer tax relief through registered retirement savings plans. We now find our mailboxes filled with letters from people cashing in their registered retirement savings plans for the annuities that are allowed. These annuities are going into the insurance companies of Canada. All the holders of RRSPs are getting back is a rate of interest return on their principal which is less than the interest rate the government will be paying on the Les Terrasses de la Chaudiere project. The principal remains for the benefit of the issuer of the annuity. That is a secondary effect respecting which we will have to offer corrective legislation. I trust that in

Protection of Borrowers and Depositors our committee deliberations we will not fall into that kind of situation with this bill.
There is another matter that causes concern. I ask this question in all sincerity. What will be the extent of the abuses leading to some chaos within the industry if borrowers arbitrarily stop payments? If this risk exists, who will lend money under that kind of program? What worries me is a newspaper report which appeared in the Globe and Mail. You get this kind of implication on this aspect of the bill, "If you think your loan rate is too high, you can simply stop making payments and force the lender to take you to court. The lender must then convince the court that the rate is not too high." If there is one problem we have in this country, it is that our judicial system is not working. It is overloaded; it is abused. Yet here we are creating a situation where if an individual feels an interest rate is too high, he can stop payment and force the lender to take him to court, further adding to the burden on the justice system and choking it.
I should like to examine the clause dealing with variable rate mortgages. It was reported almost two years ago that trust companies in Canada encountered serious liquidity problems on a break-up basis. I wonder whether the minister has considered this aspect of the legislation and the effect it will have on the industry. At the present time the industry is working within five-year term mortgages. Lending institutions borrow on five-year guaranteed income certificates and lend their money on five-year term mortgages. It is considered sound practice that the certificates be back-to-back against mortgage lending, and the mortgage companies will probably want deposits to match their obligations.
What will happen to companies which have committed themselves to five-year certificates at, say, the present rate of 1OV2 per cent, when the government comes along and changes the rules? As you know, Mr. Speaker, the government has a record of creating confusion by changing the rules in midstream, and I am afraid this is what is being done now. It has changed the rules by allowing prepayment without penalty after 36 months. What this means is that three-year term mortgages, not five-year mortgages, will be the mode of the day.
It is my belief that in the government's anxiety to get this bill before the House it has failed to consider the disruption the legislation will cause in the country. Has the minister really considered all the consequences of what he is proposing to do? For instance, how can a new family formation commit itself to a mortgage for a long-term need on the basis of three-year term renewals? Is this fair to the borrower? What assurance is there that he can afford the renewal?
We find ourselves approaching the definition of the demand term of money. It is likely that many borrowers would not have the opportunity to obligate themselves with respect to a long-term financial need when the rules of the game covering their commitment get narrower and narrower. Today, in Canada, our prime lending rate is about 4 per cent higher than

the prime lending rate in the United States-IOV2 per cent as compared to 6V2 per cent. Perhaps this country will return to sanity. Perhaps interest rates will go down and the right to own private property will be within the grasp of the rank and file of the emerging generation in Canada.
Maybe we shall accomplish a decrease in the cost of living and increase the purchasing value of the wage dollar. Maybe after the next election a measure of sanity will return to the Canadian scene and the gap between interest rates here and in the United States will narrow. Should these things happen, mortgage rates would fall and there would be a rush of prepayments on the thirty-sixth month anniversary. What happens then to the company which has covered these funds with five-year guaranteed income certificates at 1OI/2 per cent?
I ask the minister this question, also: Where does this legislation offer an incentive to drop interest rates? There is nothing here which would encourage an adjustment in the rate on the part of the lender. I suggest that this prepayment clause is likely to have serious secondary effects and would lead to three-year mortgages which offer no protection to the borrower with a long-term need. Short terms for long-term borrowing purposes represents a definite change in our system. It is my belief that even variable rate mortgages should provide for five-year fixed payments if the real interest on the unsophisticated low income borrower is to be served.
I would be the first to agree that some trust and life insurance companies have been most unfair in enforcing penalty clauses on borrowers in a rising interest market. Such greed and stupidity deserve corrective legislation. I have no argument with that idea at all. When a man managing the affairs of a corporation wants more from the community than he should clearly be asking, we have no choice but to legislate against such excessively self-interested behaviour. However, I should like to see such corrective legislation take into account all the spin-off reactions. The problem which would face the community as a result of the variable rate mortgage provisions is one of them.
In light of possible risks to the liquidity of trust companies in consequence of this legislation-and I pointed out earlier that the companies have already encountered serious liquidity problems-I wonder whether the government should not increase insurance requirements on deposits from the present $20,000 limit up to, say, $50,000 or even $100,000. I make this suggestion bearing in mind that the deposit-taking institutions are being exposed to new risks, and in these circumstances an increase in deposit insurance should be considered parallel to the present bill becoming law.
To return to the subject of the variable rate mortgage for a few moments, one of my concerns is this: what will be done with the principal amount if there is a fixed payment for a term and a variable is interjected? There is a difference here which must be considered. This brings us to the question: Under this legislation, is the review period now to be three years? How, and where, is the difference to be applied? Will it be applied to the principal outstanding, or to the interest on the transaction, or to the term of the transaction? It would
November 2, 1976

appear that a fixed term is needed for the sake of the borrower. I have already stated my view that three years is too short and that we should be looking at a five-year term as a minimum. If a borrower has not paid in enough money, he will be short at the end of the term. The little person, the unsophisticated borrower we are trying to protect, will not know how much he is short, or over. If he is sucked into a mortgage in a low interest period, perhaps he will be outside the guidelines under which he qualified for the mortgage in the first place.
For example, a man raises a $40,000 mortgage, a high ratio mortgage under which 95 per cent is advanced against it. He has a $40,000 need, and he borrows $38,000. Being a low income borrower, he will need insurance, so let us add another $400. He has now borrowed $38,400 against a $40,000 need. The mortgage is now at 96 per cent; the ratio has increased. Assume there is a 1 per cent interest change three years down the road. This will mean that this low income borrower will have a shortfall of $1,000. In this case the mortgage could be worth more than the house cost. If the market is not up, or if the house is in bad repair and the lender does not want to renew the mortgage, what is this low income borrower going to do?
One question which I do not find answered in the legislation is this. Is any provision made for a renewal clause for the protection of the borrower who finds himself in circumstances such as I have described? Or are we getting borrowers into long-term debt with a short-term demand, and is there any stability in such a situation for them? If existing mortgages can be prepaid, I submit that trust companies are opened to a new exposure which heretofore has not existed. This is why we need to know what will be the new regulations that are continually referred to throughout the bill. I think many of the unknown factors that have created the kinds of concerns I have described will become more serious as we conduct research and discuss matters with the institutions affected.
Another situation that I do not see covered by the bill is that of a company which owns its own mortgage company. A company in that position could put a loss leader on the mortgage and make an excessive profit on the price. What is the low income borrower going to do in that kind of situation when he has a short-term renewal on the mortgage? I have to ask, how far does the government want to go in protecting the unsophisticated borrower? Perhaps the answer lies in a very carefully designed educational program and in giving more assistance to our primary, secondary and tertiary educational institutions to teach the public these very simple facts of life.
Although I have not had a chance, as I have said, to hear from the various institutions affected by this bill, Mr. Speaker, I hope their concerns will be made known to us before the bill gets to committee. I have not had a chance to prepare myself in a technical way for this debate, but I have taken the opportunity to describe one or two aspects of the bill which are of concern to me.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
I think this bill is major departure from past statutory schemes, and we will have to be very careful in our deliberations to become fully aware of the legal debate that we are creating between provincial and federal jurisdiction. The provinces really do not want provincial responsibilities interfered with, and this bill, along with the Bank Act, is of concern to certain provinces. I am sure that others will also participate, on this aspect in the coming debate.
The minister goes far beyond his press releases when he submits to the people of Canada that this bill is designed to protect consumers from loan-sharking. The bill has many ramifications for the social scene, some of them very beneficial. I believe all of us have a real challenge ahead in committee to try to create out of this bill a piece of legislation that will be of benefit to the Canadian community as a whole.
There is one other small point that I overlooked, Mr. Speaker. The Post Office says that mail is the property of the receiver at the time of the postmark. The bill implies that lending institutions have an obligation to debits and credits on the date of the postmark. I do not have to remind all members of the House of the chaotic state of the postal service in this country today. We do not give the lender a fair chance to adjust to the ever-lengthening time that it takes to deliver mail or to the mail load that arrives on a Monday. Where in the legislation is it provided that the lender cannot throw away the postmark, and how are we ever going to get ourselves into a situation where we can administer a statute which provides that the postmark applies when dating debits and credits in an account? These are matters that I should like to see cleared up.
I also note that we are talking of a prime times seven factor as being a criminal rate of interest. I do not know where that came from, and some time during this debate I should like to hear the reasoning behind and the rational for a 73.5 per cent rate as being anywhere within the ball-park of a borrower's needs in Canada. I believe my time is up, Mr. Speaker, and that is about the limit of the meaningful comments that I can offer to the minister and his staff on this bill at this point in the debate.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was somewhat amused by the remarks of the last speaker when he said he had not had a chance to prepare himself for these discussions or to confer with the institutions involved. 1 find it amusing that the official critic for the opposition was critical of the time it had taken to produce this bill. Most of us have known that the bill has been in the works for a considerable period of time, and those of us who had a genuine interest took the trouble to contact the institutions and other persons interested in the bill in order to find out their opinions so as to try to provide that input.
The borrowers and depositors protection bill which we are debating today is consumer-oriented legislation which should meet with general approval. The objectives of protecting Canadian borrowers against loan-sharking and excessive interest charges, and of providing the public with more and better information for all credit deposits and transactions, should be

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors accepted by everyone. However, the intention to define strict and uniform rules to protect all borrowers and depositors could result in some disagreement as to the degree and extent to which these rules should apply. Canadians have the right to demand a high minimum standard of protection in their consumer credit ratings. The new bill requires savings institutions to disclose fully such information as the effective annual rate of interest offered and the true amount of service charges, and to credit interest to depositors' accounts at least monthly so that savers can earn the best possible return on their savings dollar. It is this point to which I shall refer later.
For the first time, all borrowers will have the unlimited right to pay off any mortgage loan at any time without penalty charges. This unlimited right of free payment will enable the borrower to retire a higher interest rate loan and to change, without penalty, to the lowest cost loan available to him or her. Under the new bill, mortgage lenders will be required to disclose fully all costs and terms of a loan at each stage of a credit transaction. Their advertising will have to spell out the rates and all the other conditions under which credit is given. Their collection methods will be regulated and subjected to criminal prosecution for harassment, threats and other coercive practices.
The BNA Act gives the federal government exclusive jurisdiction over interest, and all transactions where interest is involved must therefore be considered to be within federal jurisdiction. Banking institutions grant a major part of consumer credit and they fall exclusively within federal jurisdiction. May I add that a mortgage borrower should be fully protected at the time of a mortgage transfer. It must be made obligatory that an institution or individual selling a mortgage to another must advise at that time of any difference in the principal amount outstanding from the sum which the borrower would have normally believed to be outstanding under the principal repayment terms contained in the original agreement.
The bill is also aimed specifically at loan-sharking which is now big business in Canada, exceeding $3 billion annually and still growing. Police investigations show that real rates of interest charged by loan sharks can range as high as 1,500 per cent. However, nearly two-thirds of consumer credit is granted by institutions falling exclusively under federal jurisdiction, such as chartered banks.
I have some misgivings that certain provisions in this bill would better not be considered with the upcoming revisions to the Bank Act. I fully support the establishment of a national data bank on the extent and use of consumer credit. It is of prime importance to set up a national data bank to determine and monitor the extent and uses of consumer credit. Lenders will have to keep records and submit reports their lending activities. The data obtained will be very useful when the time comes to formulate new policies on consumer credit at both the federal and provincial levels. I assume that committee
[Mr. Herbert.)
discussion will adequately reassure those who are concerned about any invasion or loss of privacy in this particular section.
Now I would refer briefly to another of my concerns. It is always difficult when we discuss a good bill such as this not to appear to be against the bill if we criticize certain provisions. Nevertheless, the bill will be thoroughly discussed in committee, and presumably the minister is noting my comments. It was reported that the assistant deputy minister of consumer affairs said that the new consumer credit bill would encourage deposit-taking institutions to move gradually toward the daily calculation of interest payments. According to the Montreal Gazette, it was stated that a person with $200 in an account at the beginning of the month and who saves $50 a week would receive $2.31 interest that month, based on daily calculations at 8 per cent. Calculated on the monthly minimum balance basis now used at most banks, the interest payment is $1.33, a difference of about $1.00.
I know that the provisions of the bill have been changed somewhat from the documents that were originally given to us, in that now the daily balances are added so that there will be one monthly computation. Nevertheless, the effect, so far as the borrower is concerned, on his interest payments will remain the same. The previous minister of consumer and corporate affairs wrote to me as follows:
The present banking system of computing interest on the smallest balance in a six-month period permits the banks to use the full total of deposits at their disposal for that period, which they loan out at the highest attainable lending interest rate, and for which they pay the lowest possible deposit interest rate. This proposed legislation is intended to correct that imbalance.
Then he went on to say:
-there is no requirement for banks to pay any interest on any type of deposit. They do this only as an inducement to obtain funds which they can then lend at a profit.
Computing interest costs about 20 cents per calculation and entry to the account costs another 20 cents. Thus, there is a cost involved. I want to emphasize that point and I will be coming back to it. The banks have paid interest on minimum balances to keep the costs of administration down, not to reduce the cost of funds. The banks also make available a range of certificates of deposit of varying maturities from 30 days to five years on which interest is paid at rates higher than the true savings deposit rate.
Any regulation has a cost, and that cost must be paid by the consumer. So we must examine who will benefit and who will pay, and from that assess the advisability of the regulation. The banks many years ago changed their system to attempt to eliminate the fluctuating overdraft account. In its place the borrower, by demand note, stabilized his borrowings. This system, whilst costly to the heavily fluctuating account, had little or no effect on the longer term borrower. Undoubtedly, the consumer ultimately pays for all costs resulting from government regulation. I should interject here that this is not an argument against government regulation; it is just recognition of this fact before we proceed any further.
The daily addition for interest will, obviously, involve a charge that will be passed on to the customer, presumably in
November 2, 1976

the form of reduced interest rates. Such a reduction will be applicable to everyone having money on deposit at the bank. It will thus impose a penalty on those who will receive no increase in revenue from the revised method of calculation. Those who have fluctuating sums on deposit will be encouraged to delay payments. They are the least preferable accounts for the banks, yet are the only ones that may obtain some very slight benefit from the new system.
The three points that I have raised are not, under any circumstances, of such import that 1 would consider protesting to the minister about this particular bill, but they are points which I think are worth raising at this time for committee investigation. Let me reiterate those three points. Forcing the bank to compute interest on a certain basis without being able to determine what the interest rates will be, or whether, for that matter, the banks should pay any interest at all, seems to me an exercise in futility.
I also raised the subject of mortgage transfers. I did that because of my very serious concern about the manner in which mortgages have been transferred or sold between one financial institution and another to the point that the householder may not be advised, because there is nothing in the legislation to ensure that he is advised, that there could possibly have been an error in calculation, or possibly all kinds of trouble, and at the end of the period of the mortgage, whether it is 20 years or 25 years, at which time he expects he will have finished paying off the mortgage, he finds there is a principal sum outstanding. Instead of 20 years, it is now 21 or 22 years, or instead of 25 years it is 26 or 27 years. He might be too far down the road before he realizes there could have been an error of which he was not aware because there is no regulation which requires he be brought up to date.
My third point concerns privacy. The data bank is an excellent idea. I assume many people will be concerned that the information gained by this bank could become too readily available. At the present time there is no doubt that credit information is passed between groups without the knowledge of the individual involved. Although this perhaps applies more when we consider the revisions to the Bank Act, nevertheless it is also applicable to this bill. There is at the present time the practice where a borrower does not have the freedom to go from bank to bank to try to obtain the best deal. In fact, if a person should go to another bank it is almost certain that an inquiry will be made of the banker with whom the person has previously borrowed money. The borrower is likely to be told "I am sorry: we cannot lend you the money you wish". The reason, simply, is that there is co-operation-I will use that very general term-between the banks, which means there is not the same freedom for a person to shop for a loan from a bank as there is when shopping to buy a suit or, for that matter, when one goes to various stores to establish a credit account.
Perhaps it is not in the consideration of this bill that this particular point should be raised, but 1 hope that in committee
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors this matter will be explored. I have already said that my three concerns are not major concerns, but nevertheless I thought them to be of sufficient importance that they should be brought to the attention of the minister on second reading.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the previous speaker mentioned, it appears that the minister has taken a first step in the right direction. I think most of us will agree there are clauses in this bill which are worth while, but the more one reads it and the more one listens to the speeches made, the more one wonders how much good it will do in the direction in which it is going.
I listened to the two previous speakers. The argument was made that they did not have too much time to talk about the details or to examine details. But they did a heck of a good job on behalf of the finance and trust companies of this country. They have talked to them, and it appears to me that they have forgotten about the people who will be involved in these loans.

speechtext: You know about a bad loan?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Yes. I would be happy to tell you about my experience concerning what they considered to be a bad loan. These finance and trust companies are not the great heroes they are made out to be. They receive a parasitic benefit from their financial structure which should not make anyone proud to defend them, because they operate upon the misery of those who need to obtain goods and services and who can obtain those goods and services only by borrowing money at great expense.
The hon. member asked whether I have had any experience with bad loans. This is something the member perhaps should think about. I can remember when I was a miner in Timmins having a loan, as did many members of the union, with Household Finance. I remember that I owed them $300. I was maybe a little more practical than some of the other miners, because I had $300 in the bank. However, being one of the union lads, and since no one else could make their payments to the finance companies, I would not make my payments either.
When I travelled around the country raising money for the strike at that particular time, it was not unusual for me to find a representative of Household Finance waiting for me at my hotel room at 11 o'clock at night. He would harass me. He wanted me to give him $1 on account. This would not pay for the bother of harassing me, but he harassed me every night. He wanted to know who was paying for the hotel room. He wanted to get his finger on one dollar. I refused to give him one dollar, because if none of the other miners could pay one dollar, why should I pay him?
When I went to Windsor, the same thing happened. Another man was at the hotel and there was more harassment. It was

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
interesting talking to these people. They could not understand why I would not make a payment when I had the money in the bank. They did not see the principle that was involved in my not paying them. It is also interesting that when I went to pay them after the strike, I paid them off in full and they did not charge me any interest for the period during which I had made no payment: there was no penalty.
This talk about penalties and assessments is a lot of hog-wash. It depends on the circumstances. This is not really where the problem lies. The minister has considered floating the interest rate on loan companies. I was here, as I believe were some other members. When we last changed the Bank Act. This minister should be fairly familiar with some of the changes which have taken place in the Bank Act, since he comes from a family which had something to do with some of the changes in days gone by. What statement was made when we changed the interest rate from a fixed rate of 6 per cent? We were given a great deal of hogwash from the financial institutions. Everybody went around and saw them. They were well prepared. We were told that if the ceiling was taken off interest rates, they would go down. So I presumed that instead of having a 6 per cent interest rate we would have a rate of 2 per cent or 3 per cent. That did not happen.
When interest rates are not controlled, they go up and up. What really shocks me is that the minister has not talked to anybody who wants to borrow money. He has not talked to any workingmen or poor people who are going to borrow money. They do not care how it is listed; they want money and they want to know how much they will have to repay. They really do not even care how much it will cost, because if they are told it costs less over 36 months as opposed to 24 months, most of them will choose the longer period, and the difference is quite substantial. They will not go to a finance company and ask about interest rates. They are not interested in financial statements, last year's report or how much money these institutions make. They are not interested in how much they have lent, or how secure they are. These people go to finance companies and say that they want to buy a car or a trailer, that they want to take a summer vacation or buy a new stove, that they want to go on to the consumer market or, if they have sick children, to get medicine.
Working people will go into a credit office asking for a loan, and all they are concerned about is whether they are able to give a good enough story in order to get a loan. Very few of them go to a bank, and the reason is that the bank will send them immediately to see the manager. The manager will give them a big song and dance and they will not get the money they want. I once went to a finance company. The reason 1 went was that that company advertised on the radio, "Come down and see your friendly Household Finance dealer; he has money to lend you." When I needed the money, like everybody else I had that ad in the back of my mind. I went in, and I wanted the money right then. I wanted to spend the money right away. That is why I wanted to borrow it. If I had wanted to think about it for six months, I wouldn't have needed to

borrow it; I would have lost interest in whatever it was I was going to buy.
A finance company credit officer will ask where you work, how many children you have, whether you are married and how long you have been at your job, and then he will give you the money.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: Only if he finds that you are an MP.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
When I came here, members of parliament were the last people who would have any success at a financial institution. I would think they had the worst credit rating in the city of Ottawa, and probably across the country. However, years have gone by and, hopefully, our credit rating is better. It would not have mattered even if a member of parliament went to Household Finance. They probably would not have got a loan from a bank, but if they had gone to Household Finance, even they might have been able to borrow.
Interest rates were never a problem. That did not matter, and it does not matter now. The only thing that matters is whether a loan can be made and how many months it will take to pay it back. Why do interest rates not matter? I have not gone to a finance company for many years, but interest rates do not matter because people assume that the government has fixed an interest rate limit for finance companies. If people borrow more money, we get into the mortgage field and there is a different rate, but the government is going to take care of that.
What will happen under the proposal of the minister? I wonder if he ever really thought about it. A worker will go to a finance company and he will be asked whether he is married. If the answer is yes, the credit officer will write down a couple of figures. The worker will then be asked whether he has any children, and another figure will go down. He will then be asked whether he owns his own house and whether it is mortgaged, and a few more figures will be put down. He will be asked whether he has a car and how long he has been at his job, and a few more figures will go down. Then the worker will be told that he is not a good risk and that his rate will be, for example, 24 per cent.
Another fellow might come in with a different set of answers, and taking the minister's "x", "y" and "z" factors into account, his rate might be 17 per cent. So there is another price to pay for this latter applicant. Everyone who goes into a finance company and has a different set of "x", "y" and "z" factors will have a different rate, from the criminal rate right down to a rate at which even the finance company cannot borrow from the bank. The only thing the finance company will have to do is periodically declare its costs, which will have already been negotiated. It is true that a person might be able to go down the street and get a better deal, and that will mean that people might shop around. That might be a good thing. But it seems to me that we are not talking about downtown Montreal, Vancouver or Toronto. In many cases we are talking about places where there is only one financial institution. In those cases, a person may find that he is paying a different rate from his friend, and his friend is paying a different rate
November 2, 1976

from another friend. Everybody who goes there will have a personalized rate.
The minister will make darned sure that the risk will not be higher than the return, and for this reason, as 1 see it, he will allow all kinds of rates if people want to negotiate their rates on the basis of these many factors. I think that would be a disaster. The less capable a person is of understanding the rate he is to pay, the more financial institutions will be able to charge him, and he will be charged a high rate. Those who are astute with regard to business practices will not go to finance companies in the first place. They will go to a bank. However, if people are not astute, they are poorly equipped to deal with the information the minister says he is going to provide and they will pay more. Is it not possible for us to go back to a fixed rate?
Hon. members have talked about a criminal rate. When we talk about 73 per cent, we are talking about downtown Toronto, Vancouver or Montreal where the mafia will put a person into a pair of cement shoes if they do not make their payments. That is loan-sharking. Let us not confuse loansharking with what happens in the normal course of events. The loan-sharking the minister talks about might be totally different from my understanding of that term, but to me loan-sharking is an unconscionable transaction brought about because a person cannot borrow from anywhere else and he has to pay whatever the situation demands. If necessary, he may have to sign over his life. When the general public reads about loan-sharking, they read about people who pay with their lives.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Over the past year I have been reading about investigations in the city of Montreal into the loan-sharking practices which have been taking place there. What is loansharking in the city of Toronto? In Toronto that activity takes place on skid row and people pay with their lives or at interest rates which are sometimes 100 per cent per day. Today a person might borrow $100, and tomorrow he will have to repay $200. When you are borrowing for an emergency, payments of that kind are sometimes warranted. Companies do not borrow this way when they are a little short of cash for a contract and they need a few dollars. That is not loan-sharking as we know it, unless they are dealing with the mafia or the underworld.
I am sure the minister is not prepared to say the legislation will stop that. He has not even taken the precaution of making it mandatory that everyone who enters into any kind of loan arrangement should be licensed. These arrangements that the general public understand as loan-sharking occur in pool rooms and such places. The minister is a lawyer, and I presume he has handled not only corporation law but has acted
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors as defence counsel. If he has, he will know the kind of people the general public consider to be in the loan-sharking business and will no doubt have defended some of their victims. But maybe he has a new definition of loan-sharking, Mr. Speaker, just as he has a new definition of "reasonable interest," meaning whatever can be charged, taking the risk into consideration.
The committee should look carefully at the general problem of interest rates. I consider, as I think anyone with a protestant work ethic background would, that a 10 per cent interest rate is usury.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext: That is an anti-Catholic remark.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
As a young person I was exposed to the Protestant ethic. The Roman Catholic philosophy probably has the same kind of ethic and believes that more than 10 per cent interest is thievery. Yet today there are very few house mortgages-and a house is a necessity, not a luxury-where the interest rate is not in excess of 10 per cent.
To get away from dogma, Mr. Speaker, I suppose we could think back to biblical times when Christ threw the moneylenders out of the temple. I used the Protestant ethic as an example because that is the one I was raised under; but I suppose moneylending goes back a long way. Lending money as a result of somebody else's misfortune has never been an honourable profession, but if there is to be any justification for it, then it seems to me the minister has to do a number of things. In the last election campaign the Liberals promised that moneylenders would be licensed in order to control chequebuying and loan-sharking. I suppose loan-sharking, in common terminology, extends to that dangerous level of the criminal element of our society where people go for money they cannot get elsewhere. If I were to put an interest rate on loan-sharking, I would certainly put 10 per cent in that category; but apparently the minister does not. In the last election campaign the Liberals also indicated that by the end of 1974 they would increase the number of consumer storefront offices to 20. I do not know whether they have done that, but I doubt it very much.
Perhaps we could learn something from the election campaign in the United States. Even in that great, free enterprise empire they are talking about trying to pay their way. Mr. Carter has said it should be mandatory that government expenditures be justified for programs included in the budget.

speechtext: What do you think we are doing?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES, BILL C-16, CONSIDERATION RESUMED ON THE MOTION, MR. ABBOTT, FOR SECOND READING AND REFERENCE TO THE STANDING COMMITTEE ON HEALTH, WELFARE AND SOCIAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
We are not doing it in this bill. We do not even indicate to people that it may be worth their while to pay for things out of the money they have, rather than the money they may earn tomorrow. The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) advanced a very good idea, as a private member, that many of us supported, for a card called "Cashex". He suggested that if you took this card to a store when you made a purchase, you should get a premium for paying cash. Unfortunately, in these days many stores are not equipped to deal with cash and only have credit card facilities.

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
I think the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) has an obligation to set up an agency that will inform the people of the advantages of paying cash and will advise individuals how to handle their income in the best way possible. Through advertising the consumer is encouraged to go out and buy, buy, buy. The agency would be able to advise people of the cost of borrowing, and in some cases might even be able to talk them out of making purchases.
I spoke earlier about the role of the banks, Mr. Speaker. When you apply to a bank for a loan, first of all the accountant asks if you have any money in the bank. 1 can never understand why you would borrow money if you already have some in the bank. At one time I wanted to buy a new car. I had a $5,000 bond in the bank, so I cashed it. I did not spend all of it on the car. Later I found that it cost me $1,500 or $2,000 to cash that bond, whereas if I had borrowed the money I would have come out ahead; the interest rate would have offset the income tax, but nobody explained that to me. A consumer credit advisory bureau would explain to people the best way of handling their money. I do not think the average person has this knowledge.
If the minister is honestly interested in this problem, he should spend a few days talking to the working poor of the country and to the middle income people who are earning good salaries. I think the very poor should not be allowed to borrow money under any circumstances: we should be giving them money instead of asking them to borrow it at interest rates which are unconscionable. If someone is living on welfare or drawing an allowance under one of the federal or provincial programs, it is not always their fault if they have to borrow money from a finance company; it is ours. In my opinion they should not be allowed to borrow. If they can establish the need, there should be an agency to advise them.
To be fair, some agencies and family services in Ontario will help with roof repairs and heating repairs. If someone living on welfare needs money for this sort of thing, it is made available in addition to welfare. That is how it should be handled. You should not ask a person to go to IAC, Household Finance or the friendly finance company for money at high interest, because such borrowing acts like a snowball; pretty soon such people are deeper and deeper in trouble until they must use the bankruptcy structure which this government recently provided.
Incidentally, I heard a story about a young chap who borrowed money from a finance company to go into bankruptcy. He went to a finance company and said, "Lend me $300 to enable me to go bankrupt." The question is, why should a finance company lend him money if he intends to go bankrupt a couple of days later? But the company did lend it. I will tell you why: the guy borrowing the money said, "I will pay you back." This story highlights something very interesting. In the high income brackets of this country you will find cheats of all kinds, those who cheat on a huge scale, those who cheat on income tax, etc. The little guy at the bottom of the scale who works in the mine or factory does not cheat on anything. He

has no expense account; he cannot write anything off against income tax. That does not apply to people in the higher income brackets who can even write off their meals. You see them all over Ottawa, eating in restaurants and writing their meals off against income tax. But you and I, Mr. Speaker, as members of parliament are not quite in that position. We are more like the wage earner; we pay for our meals and do not write them off.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this debate. I want to say, as have other speakers of my party, that we support the principles of this bill and will co-operate with the minister in moving it through the House of Commons and into committee. We will, of course, have a number of questions to ask when it gets into committee. Hopefully, with the co-operation of other members, we will be able to make some improvements.
Having listened to all the speeches so far in this debate, I think it is important that we remember-and it is obvious from looking at it-that this bill was not brought into the House just to go after so-called loan sharks or the hard-core criminal element which deals in lending money to certain people who as some hon. members said, must pay back at 100 per cent or more interest or, in extreme cases, be killed or, in less extreme cases, be beaten up. It is in fairness to the vast majority of honest people in the financial institutions of this country that we say that now.
It is very easy, especially if you listen to what some hon. members have said and what sometimes appears in the media, to come to the conclusion that this bill is designed to wipe out all criminal activity in this country. Clearly, it is not designed to do that. As my friend, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), said a few minutes ago, it will not do that. Of course it will not.
What is this bill trying to do? No one can expect it to wipe out the hard-core criminal element. It may be helpful in at least making it more difficult for the quasi-criminal loan outlet which is using laundered money to operate rapaciously or unfairly. However, what it is really aimed at is establishing a more reasonable environment within which people in lower income levels or in need of large loans can borrow money with more certainty, knowing the deal they are entering into. That is what this bill is all about.
Some hon. members have pointed out in quite a compelling way that there are problems when unsophisticated borrowers go to finance companies. They have referred to problems when people are in desperate straits through no fault of their own and have to get money very quickly. It is no good telling them they are in no position to borrow. They are in no position to do anything but borrow, unless they steal. That is the dilemma they are in. These people will need money from time to time. There will always be people to whom the wisest advice you' could give would be, "Don't borrow any money." They are often the people who desperately need money, and they have to know what the deal is.

Some speakers before me, including the last speaker, suggested that the bill should include a vast counselling service so that everybody who contemplates taking out a loan could receive advice on whether they should be taking such a step and, if so, what would be the best kind of loan to take out. It would be nice if we had the resources in this country to give that kind of counselling to everyone who is likely to borrow. But there are practical difficulties as well as philosophic ones in the way of such a proposal.
The practical difficulties are extraordinary when one considers that in 1950 the amount of consumer credit outstanding was $1.2 billion, representing 10.2 per cent of total personal expenditure in that year, and that by the end of 1974 the figure had risen to $20.6 billion, representing 25.8 per cent of the year's consumer spending. To seriously consider that the bill before us can make provision for a counselling service for the benefit of anybody and everybody who wants to get a loan in this country is, in my view, being unrealistic. I am not at all sure that from a philosophical point of view it is wise to take the attitude that people cannot make their own decisions about their affairs. Moreover, I am not at all sure the people concerned would thank us one bit if we set up an expensive bureaucracy to advise them how to manage their personal financial transactions.
I want to emphasize that the bill is designed to create an atmosphere of fairness and certainty in connection with legitimate dealings within the financial market. It is not designed to wipe out the hard-core criminal or even to wipe out the quasi-criminal. It is important to remember that many people who borrow money do not borrow it from financial institutions. They borrow it from each other. A newly-married couple borrows money from parents-in-law or from relatives. Young people borrow from older friends, and friends borrow from each other.
A large number of people who may in the course of a lifetime make only one or two loans are, nonetheless, within the contemplation of the bill before us. I bring this to the attention of the House so that we might avoid the danger of slipping into the assumption that anybody who makes a loan is in the position of being a powerful financial institution knowing exactly what the ground rules are.
I am glad to see the minister in the House, as he has been throughout most of the debate. I say to him, through you, Mr. Speaker, that the measure is a complex one. We understand the reason for its complexity; it deals with a complex subject. But as I was saying, it will govern lenders who are by no means in the position of being powerful financial institutions in receipt of expert advice. It applies to loans made between families or friends, which form part of the financial arrangements made by a great many people in this country. This being the case, we must look carefully at the details of these provisions to ensure that in seeking to create a climate of greater fairness and certainty we do not impose burdens on innocent lenders or upon innocent borrowers which we did not intend to impose.
