subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
that Bill C-204, to amend the Canada Elections Act (permanent voters' list), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to be here this afternoon speaking on this problem. I am somewhat out of breath: we were sitting in the committee on justice this after-
Permanent Voters' List
noon and I was still questioning Mr. Terry at five minutes to five. I shall be very quick. I have notes for a short speech about the benefits which, hopefully, would flow from this bill and I trust hon. members opposite will agree to let it go to committee.
The preparation of a voters' list is one of the most important stages in a general election. The fair and comprehensive compilation of such a list is one aspect of electoral reform to which a great deal of time has been devoted, yet this remains an area of differing opinions. To adequately answer the question as to which system has the least drawbacks and most advantages, we should look at this problem within the framework of some criteria. The first and foremost criterion is the inclusion of the greatest number of names of eligible voters and, conversely, of the least possible number of eneligible voters. The second criterion is the relative cost of preparing the list of voters.
My bill, Mr. Speaker, calls for a continuous, permanent list in which the initiative for registration should lie with the individual. This is not to say that the Crown should not exercise some influence. As is the experience in many American states, unless there is some degree of compulsion or scheme of intensive publicity campaigns, reliance on voter initiative is unlikely to produce a very complete list. What we would have is a combination of systems placing the primary responsibility on the voters to register themselves, and also introducing a considerable measure of follow-up action and publicity by election officials to ensure that the greatest possible number of voters do in fact exercise their right. Two examples of this system would be New Zealand and Great Britain.
It is my feeling that Canadian election campaigns are unduly prolonged, not so much to allow the campaign strategists to exercise their talents but more to allow for an election list to be compiled as accurately as possible in a given time. Surely, Mr. Speaker, a permanent, continuous list would alleviate some of the cumbersome and time-consuming qualities our system now exhibits. A permanent, continuous list would indeed be fair for all parties and allow campaign organizers to have a copy of a list of voters at any given time and allow more time for workers and supporters to canvass prospective voters.
In a study in 1968, the Canadian representation commissioner found that:
The system of continuous electoral rolls currently in use in the Commonwealth of Australia, including the method of compulsory registration on the part of the electors, can be adapted for use in federal elections in Canada to reduce the time required for the holding of elections and to provide improved facilities for voting by electors-
There have been arguments, Mr. Speaker, that to effectively and adequately institute a continuous, permanent voters' list involves the outlay of a sufficient amount of money. Firstly, this conclusion has been arrived at not out of practice but out of guesswork. Not since 1935, by way of the Dominion Franchise Act of 1934, have we tried a permanent list. By the chief

November 2, 1976
Permanent Voters' List
electoral officer's own words, the permanent list was not that disfunctional. Many feel that in order to set up a continuous, permanent voters' list an electoral office must be set up in each constituency. I do not think this is necessary, and in order to cut down the expenses one central office could surely handle compilation of a list that effectively puts the onus on the voter to register himself. Naturally, an annual update of the list would have to occur and then review officers could be sent out to the constituencies to update the list, making deletions and noting changes.
One way, Mr. Speaker, of facilitating the actual registration voters could be by way of incorporating a section on our personal income tax forms. The names and related documentation could easily be handled by the revenue department's computer with considerable ease, thus alleviating some of the paperwork, added confusion and extra expenditures. I am told the cost of conducting the enumeration in the last federal election in 1974 cost $29 million. 1 think one can question not only the cost but the accuracy of the enumeration and the number of individuals disenfranchised in each election because of haphazard enumeration. A permanent list with yearly updates by way of constituency reviews can surely incorporate the greatest number of eligible voters at any given time. Surely this is what we should be striving for in electoral reform, Mr. Speaker.
Not since 1938, under the Dominion Elections Act, has the process of registering voters changed. I am not saying the permanent list is the answer to all the problems, but 1 do think this bill should be referred to committee for study. Perhaps there we can carefully and accurately ascertain which system best suits our needs. I do not think it is fair to dismiss the permanent voters' list as expensive. It does hold some redeeming value in the enumerating process, and I think with a carefully constructed combination of primary responsibility on the voter, and exact follow-up action on a yearly basis, we can have a system that will be envied.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make reference to a comparison of the percentage of the total voting age populations which were registered on official voters' lists. The most recent figures I could obtain are from the 1966 census, but I think they will nonetheless explain my point. At that time the voting age was 21 years. The number of voting age population, according to the 1966 census, was 11,260,202. The number of electors on voters' lists for that time was 10,274,904, a difference of 985,298, all of whom were disenfranchised. I am well aware that those institutionalized or those classified as transients sometimes lose their vote, but a figure close to one million causes me some concern. I have to ask myself how thoroughly our present enumeration is being carried out, and for that reason alone I think this bill should be referred to committee.
Finally, I should just like to say this, Mr. Speaker. In getting the bill into committee, one aspect we will have to examine, and one of the matters we have talked about in the privileges and elections committee last session, is the length of time of elections. We are managing to knock a few days off at
[Mr. Reynolds.)
times, but the election now going on in the province of Quebec is going to last 28 days. I think that should be the maximum time. A month is more time than we need for an election in the electoral process of this country.
The cost of keeping a permanent voters' list may be more than an enumeration every two, three or four years whenever an election is called. The cost saved to the public purse in cutting down the length of an election would, however, be tremendous. It would also mean that parliament would not have to be in recess for such a long time. Therefore, I hope hon. members on the other side will see fit to send this bill to committee. We did not come up with a final answer last session, but if the bill does go back to committee we may be able to come up with a solution this time which will save the voters of this country another long election, whenever it may be.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR PERMANENT VOTERS' LIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the criteria set out by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds). We should evaluate the various systems of preparing electoral rolls in existence in Canada. The two criteria which should be used to evaluate the systems, or which could be used in the registration procedures, would be as follows. The first criterion is the inclusion of the greatest number of names eligible, and the least possible number of ineligible names. The second criterion, of course, is the relative cost of preparing the list of voters.
Always keep in mind, Mr. Speaker, that even with the most perfect list of voters that we could have, it still would not guarantee a good voter turnout. This is the experience in the United States today, where they estimate they might get 50 per cent of the voters out. I am told they do have obligatory and continual permanent voting, if you will, in many of the states, if not all of them, though I do not know whether that is the federal fact. I think we should surely take this into consideration in our discussion of a permanent voters' list and its place in Canadian society.

Now, Mr. Speaker, let us first examine the features of the different voter registration systems. Voter registration has been accepted in western democratic countries as a protection against fraud. It makes possible advance identification of such voters who are really entitled to cast their ballots so that we may be sure that only they will exercise their rights to vote. With this in mind, democratic countries have enacted various legislation providing for voter registration.

Voter registration systems were gradually adopted in most countries in the latter half of the nineteenth century and arose out of a general need to bring administrative order to the election process. Some countries created systems that placed responsibility for registration on individual voters, but Canada made public authority, not the individual, legally responsible for the burden of voter registration. This distiction between government initiated systems and those which depend on the
November 2, 1976

personal initiative of voters is a fundamental dimension that can be used to characterize voter registration systems.
Let us consider two kinds of government-initiated registration systems. In countries where there is a register of internal migration, a list of eligible voters is generated from information recorded in a general population register. In West Germany, for example, the state maintains a continuous record of important demographic events for each citizen. This record includes birth, death, marriage, divorce and migration. It is the recording of this last event, migration, that makes possible the compilation of an extremely accurate electoral register. Each German citizen must register changes of residence with the local authorities. There is a fine for non-compliance. If the move is between cities, the citizen must notify the officials in both places. All of this information is recorded in a central municipal office. An electoral official examines each new registration to see that that registrant is qualified to vote. If so, the name and credentials are placed in a special file of qualified voters. At the time of an election, the file is used to print lists of qualified voters. Similar systems of automatic registration are used in Sweden and in Switzerland.
I do not know if the Canadian people as a whole would readily accept this kind of documentation of their citizens travelling between cities. I would remind my colleagues that in Canada you can go from coast to coast without registering, so long as you are a citizen, and even if you are not, no one will bother you. 1 do not know if it is in the nature of a Canadian citizen to accept this kind of documentation with the purpose of finding out where you are and where you are going, ail in the name of voter registration, in the name of controlling the movement of citizens. Perhaps it is acceptable in Europe, but I suggest that it would not be totally acceptable to those of us who live in Canada.
[ Translation]
The second registration formula initiated by the government is a kind of census carried out by a government agency. This is the case in England and in Canada where there is no mandatory registration and no internal migration. In England a fresh list of electors is drawn every year for each Federal constituency. The municipal clerk sends application forms through the mail to each household in the constituency. The head of the household has the responsibility under the law to list all qualified voters residing with him and mail back the list to the municipal clerk.

If the response to this direct mail canvass is not satisfactory, the clerk sends door-to-door canvassers to those areas with low response rates. The list developed through the canvass is used for any and all elections held during the year following the end of the canvass and the official closing of the next list on February 15 of the following year. In Canada, a new list of qualified voters is developed prior to each federal election. A complete door-to-door canvass is made in urban areas, which are defined by law as cities of 5,000 or more. In rural areas the
Permanent Voters' List
lists are made up by registration officials through a door-to-door canvass or other inquiries.
Government-initiated registration systems can be further distinguished by their effectiveness in registering the eligible electorate. I note that the hon. member in his remarks to us in the House referred to the success of a permanent list. I think he should be made aware of the results of the permanent lists which are used in England. Systems of automatic registration obviously are most effective, depending only on the accuracy of the population register. In countries with a compulsory registration system, the electoral list should be virtually a complete accounting of the potential by qualified electorate, minus people in transit at the time of an election. The canvassing techniques used in Canada and England also produce lists which accurately mirror the potential electorate. The Chief Electoral Officer of Canada, who supervises the conduct of federal elections, estimates that for the 1972 election approximately 90 per cent of all eligible voters were registered.
What about the British lists? These are permanent voters' lists. How do they compare with the system currently in use in Canada? We should look at the two so as to compare them. First of all, the British lists are a little less accurate, depending on when an election is held. In Canada, registration is conducted only before each election and the lists are no more than Vh weeks old by election day. In Britain, registration is done annually and the lists are closed on February 15 of each year. No new registrations are added after the closing date, but people who move after the close of the lists may vote from their former residence in parliamentary elections. This means that elections held toward the end of the 12-month period in which the electoral register is in effect will be conducted under old, and thus more inaccurate, list. An election held in December, for example, would be conducted with a list 9lA months old. Nonetheless, the electoral register still accurately lists approximately 85 per cent of the people living in a constituency even at the end of its one-year life. I suggest that this is nowhere near the 98 per cent which we have currently in Canada.
A study of the accuracy of the 1966 register in England produced the following findings. On the qualifying date, October 10, 1965, they were able to list 96 per cent of all the people who were eligible to vote, not 98 per cent but 96 per cent to begin with. When the register came into force on February 16, 1966, the list was down to an accuracy of 93 per cent. Halfway through the life of the register in August, 1966, it was down to 89 per cent and, as I mentioned before, at the end of the life of the register on February 15, 1967, it was down to 85 per cent. I suggest that this is not acceptable when we can get more up-to-date lists.
Registration systems in which the burden for initiating registration lies with the individual citizen appear to be limited to the United States, as I mentioned earlier, to the province of British Columbia where the hon. member for Burnaby-Rich-mond-Delta comes from, to France, and to a few Latin American countries.

Who is to be entrusted with the gathering of all this information, always keeping in mind that here in Canada at least we have government-initiated programs where the government is the authority which gets this information, not the individual? We know that the returning officers appoint two enumerators in each urban polling division. These enumerators are chosen from lists supplied by the two candidates who have received the highest number of votes in the preceding election. This bipartisan feature is intended to serve as a check against attempts to falsify the registration lists. The enumerators are paid a flat fee of $35, plus an addition of ten cents for each name added to the list. Most enumerators earn between $50 and $60.
As to the method of gathering information, the enumerators must visit each dwelling place in the polling division. If there is no one at home on their first visit, they must leave a card stating the date and time they will call again. If there are two visits, one must occur between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m. and the other between 7 p.m. and 10 p.m. For each person enumerated they must leave a form notifying the individual that he or she will be included on the list of eligible voters.
So here we have a counter check by which to make sure that the people who are directly involved in the voting process will know not only that they are eligible but that they are on the list, so that on election day they will be able to take part in the democratic process. In Canada the information obtained by the enumerators includes only name, address and occupation, I would point out, again, that at least to me this information about internal migration in our country is just not acceptable. No signature is obtained from the elector, nor can enumerators demand identification such as a driver's licence, birth certificate and the like.
It is possible for aliens such as United States citizens or citizens from any other country living in Canada to appear on the enumerator's list. They are not required to obtain information directly from each eligible voter but many obtain it from other sources such as members of the family. The printed list sent to candidates and voters serves a number of purposes. It is primarily a device for ensuring accuracy. People listed incorrectly can have corrections made at a later revising period. At the same time, those voters such as resident aliens listed improperly may be challenged, and those left off the list may be added.
Since the list is so widely available and a common object of public knowledge, it is believed there is little opportunity for fraudulent registrations. The printed lists also serve an important information function, noting the times and locations for revising the lists, procedures for challenges and corrections, information about advance polling and the location of polling places. The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta mentioned that in Canada a new list is prepared for each federal election. Indeed it is. The lists are used for that election only and then discarded. This system has been in use since 1920

with the exception of the 1935 general election when permanent lists were used.
This was repealed in 1938, allegedly because of the excessive cost and the inaccuracy of the voters' lists obtained. I refer to the criteria, once again, which the hon. member has raised. Let us evaluate the various systems for preparing electoral rolls in existence in Canada. Two criteria, as was mentioned, would be used to evaluate the registration procedures. The first criterion is the inclusion of the greatest number of names of eligible voters, and the least possible number of the ineligible.
The second criterion is the relative cost of preparing the list of voters. From the first criterion, which is that of the quantity of names of eligible votes included, and the accuracy of the list, it seems a system of continuous lists with compulsory registration by voters is the best system. Yet the only continuous list in existence in Canada, which is the British Columbia system, does not require compulsory registration. Experience in many American states indicates that unless there is some degree of compulsion, or a scheme of intensive publicity campaigns, reliance on voter initiative is unlikely to produce a very complete list.
Now I should like to quote from the same source as the hon. member. In his report on Methods of Registration of Electors and Absentee Voting (1968), the representation commissioner of Canada commented on the problems of a system employing voluntary registration as the sole method of updating the rolls. He said:
Because of the general apathy with which electors view registration, few avail themselves of the opportunity to register or correct existing registration either by personal attendance before, or by mailing the prescribed forms to, a registrar, in the period between elections.
When a general election is imminent and during the short period of time between the date an election is called and polling day, there is an impetus for some electors to register. However, such a last minute rush tends to cause the system to break down under its own weight. It is impossible to deal adequately with a large number of new registrations at a date so close to polling day.
It is too soon to make a judgment on the system of a permanent list drawn up by enumeration established by Quebec and Prince Edward Island. Generally speaking, the free election enumeration procedure in effect in Canada and in most provinces has been satisfactory. This system produces what is surely the most up-to-date list of voters possible. The main source of error on the list is not so much the omission of the eligible as the inclusion of the ineligible, especially the non-citizens.
With regard to the second criterion, which is that of the cost of making the lists, it is the temporary list system that is the least costly. If I may quote the figures of the hon. member, he said that the cost in 1974 was $29 million. 1 ask myself and I ask you, Mr. Speaker, and other members of this House what would be the cost of permanent, ongoing lists if they were more than the $29 million which has been quoted?

How many people were deprived of their right to vote simply because they were away on holiday when all of a sudden the election was called.

In any case, Mr. Speaker, I do not want to dwell on the subject. I hope the House can at least allow this bill to go to the appropriate committee. 1 want to assure my colleagues on both sides of the House if they want I will send them all the documentation to know how a permanent voters' list could be put together in this country. I have it in both official languages. I will be pleased to have copies made of it and distributed.
I remember the case of a lady of almost 90 years of age;- not at the time of the 1975 by-elections because at that time those things did not happen-she cried because her name had been left out in the list when the enumerator had gone around. When the list was revised and the error was noticed, it was too late to do anything about it. There again, there have been many cases of injustice.
There is a form bearing No. 7 and entitled "Enumerators' Notice to Elector". A candidate never knows how many of those forms are in the possession of the returning officer. The social insurance number is not even indicated on those forms. How can there be any control? Not that I want to cast any doubt on the integrity of the returning officers, but the fact remains that there are always a few dishonest people who manage to get those documents and make counterfeits. I can assure you that there are many ways to get votes and win an election dishonestly.
A permanent voters' list would, finally and once and for all, enable us to have honest elections in Canada. And, 1 am convinced of it, when my colleagues read the document I will send them, they will see that the truth exists and that facts prove it.
Of course, when we talk about a permanent list, in my opinion and according to the working paper that I have here, it is out of the question to have a yearly registration. It is also out of the question to change everything completely. Certain people do not want to register because they do not want to be checked upon, like the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) said so well. Of course, they are not being checked upon. If you move and go from one province to another, your health insurance card and other proofs of identity follow you.
I think that we must eliminate this fear factor. These papers could easily include a voter card. I have heard people talk for many years. I have heard so-called experts talk about voter cards and permanent lists, but no sincere person ever dared submit something concrete. I am not saying that it is perfect. I am not saying that it is 100 per cent. But if it can help my colleagues, we should at least accept that this bill be referred to the appropriate authority, and then, in the light of suggestions from all sides of the House and of this working paper, Parliament would be able to decide whether we should adopt a permanent voters list in Canada and how it should be done. Perhaps the two countries which best illustrate the use of the permanent voters' list are Australia and New Zealand. There is also West Germany. In Australia, however, there is the additional factor of a penalty for those who fail to vote. I think hon. members will recall that through many elections in Australia, as in Canada, one party stays in for very long periods of time. Indeed before the last Australian general election the Governor General saw fit to remove the prime minister from office. He then dissolved parliament and called another election.
In Australia the permanent voters' list is revised at a specific time-it is like bringing in your car to be tuned; voters get tuned at certain times of the year. In the instance I have cited the election came six months too soon and, as a result, many Australians were disfranchised. This points out the weakness of the system, Mr. Speaker; to be effective it should be kept up almost on a monthly basis.
One of the most ideal countries in the world for the operation of a permanent voters' list would be the United States. It is ironic that we should be discussing this today when they are in the throes of an election. Every four years in the United States there is a presidential election. Even if a president should die during his term, or be removed from office, the vice president carries on until the term expires. It happens quite frequently in that country that the elected President and the Senate and House of Representatives are of the opposite parties. I think

the last time the president was of the same party as the house was during President Johnson's term. The United States is one of the few countries in the world that could use a permanent voters' list on a federal basis. Some hon. members have stated that there is a permanent voters' list in the United States, but I would point out that it does not apply to all states; there are two or three states with no such system.
It has been mentioned already that Canada tried this system in July, 1934. But in the 1935 election very few people came out to vote, using the normal procedures. In the end many of the members who were elected on that occasion had to go out and find the people and get them registered because there was no proper system. As the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Parent) pointed out, the arrangement had to be abandoned.
Some hon. members have touched on the question of costs. The hon. member for St. Catharines hedged on the costs of the 1974 election and the possible cost of the next one. But, Mr. Speaker, I do not mind putting a figure on it. It will be anywhere from $30 million to $32 million. As the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) suggested, by reducing the election period from 60 days to 47 days, $2 million could be saved. But here we are playing around with $4 million to $6 million for a permanent voters list.
It is also likely that an additional 1,200 to 1,300 civil servants would be required to keep a permanent voters list up to date. If we want to hold costs down we must think of these things.
The hon. member for Hochelaga (Mr. Lavoie) referred to the problem of people being missed by enumerators. A permanent voters list would correct that problem.
I would like to ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to join with me in trying to find a way to take care of the absentee vote which is something we do not have in the present Federal Elections Act. The matter of the proxy vote was brought up some years ago by a former member for Coast Chilcotin, Mr. Paul St. Pierre. I do not mind saying that I assisted him as a returning officer and helped him to prepare the proposal. It was milked down considerably in committee. When the matter came before the House of Commons for a vote, it was not in the form I had anticipated. The proxy vote has its weaknesses. It has been abused in two elections. I came across a number of abuses in the 1972 election, and I know there were abuses in the 1974 election.
Hon. members should know that any permanent voters' list would involve high expenses. We ought to be most concerned about those who must be away from home, who are travelling or on holiday and, under the present Canada Elections Act, are denied the privilege of voting, and not so greatly concerned about a permanent voters list.
Let me touch on something else. We spoke of enumerators, but now I raise the matter of participation. We all know what it means, especially when we run political campaigns. Instead

of being concerned about a permanent voters' list, it would be better if people would take a greater interest in the political process. I would hope that as many Canadians as possible would participate in any general election, would think highly of those who are elected, and take a great interest in individual candidates.
It is possible that if you do away with enumeration and the enumeration system you will take many hundreds of people out of circulation. The hon. member for Hochelaga touched on various subjects and talked about voters' lists. During my six years as a returning officer I knew of no instance of any returning officer anywhere in Canada being involved in underhand dealings involving voters' lists and wrongfully giving out information pertinent to the electoral process. I want to make that point clear because it is possible that allegations of bad dealing have been made by some who could not back up their statements.
As a former electoral officer I have great respect for my former chief, the Chief Electoral Officer, and for all my other colleagues who worked with me during that period.

I am coming to the final part of my remarks. I emphasize, as has been said, that at election time we deal with people. It is all very well to have a permanent voters' list. You can have 21 million or X number on your voters' list; but that is not what counts. What counts is the people who turn out to vote. It does not matter how many are on the list; what matters is how many people become involved in the actual election. That is why our system is so good. The enumerator reminds people they have a job to do, that they must come forward and play their part in the election. Let us not forget that the ballot in Canada is still secret. We are very fortunate in being able to step forward and cast our vote in secret. It is a privilege. I particularly wanted to make that point.
Let me deal with another point which may not have been mentioned. Statistics for the years 1965 to 1971 show that 50 per cent of the people of Canada tend to change their residences within a certain period. We are somewhat nomadic. I understand the figure recently rose to 70 per cent, and the most recent figure may even approach 75 per cent. Our people are not just confinned to Canada, Mr. Speaker; we are to be found all over the world. We are travelling, as never before-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner adjournment, as a result of a moment of enthusiasm on the part of some of my colleagues, I was interrupted. One of the consequences of that is that it compels hon. members to hear again what I was saying at the end of my remarks before private members' hour began.
In response to what some hon. members have said throughout the debate so far, keeping in mind that sometimes, perhaps out of thoughtlessness, the thrust of the remarks has almost been an attack on all those who are in lending institutions in this country, and in the financial part of our commercial world, I was pointing out that, next to lawyers, money lenders over the centuries, as literature shows us, have been most unpopular.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Just speak for yourself.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
That remark was made before the dinner hour. You will have to come up with some new ones now.
The point I am making in all seriousness is that in the commercial world in which we live, and in the economic system which we have, there are legitimate lenders and there are legitimate borrowers. Our particular economic system would probably be in severe difficulty if we reverted to the narrow concepts of the Middle Ages and referred to all those who are in lending institutions or who loan money, whether it be privately in terms of their private friendships or family relationships, or in the commercial world, as a group within the community that are worthy to be the subject of vituperation and attack by either the media, members of parliament, other politicians, or frustrated or antagonistic members of the public. I want to emphasize that almost all of us at one time or another have to borrow money.
1 want to re-emphasize the point that I made before the dinner hour. It is my view that this bill, despite a great deal of talk about loan-sharking and some talk about the criminal element in the country, is not likely to do very much to cure
November 2, 1976

crime in Canada. The real purpose of the bill, as I see it, is to bring about an environment of certainty so that those who do borrow and those who lend clearly understand the arrangement and the deal.
I have a great deal of sympathy, especially with those in a low income position, who often do not have the business experience or sophistication in commercial matters to be able to judge competently when and under what circumstances they should enter into a particular loan transaction.
I said before the dinner hour that one of the suggestions made during the debate was that we should establish, at public expense, agencies which would advise all those who borrowed so that they would not make mistakes. This is probably impracticable because of the amount of borrowing which takes place in this country. I also pointed out that one must consider the philosophic implications of such a course, one which might involve the protection of the public to such an extent that it was difficult for them to exercise any free choice at all; I doubt very much whether the public would thank us for setting up a bureaucracy which, in the end, might be an important factor in determining not only where people could best borrow but whether, in the circumstances, they ought to borrow at all.
It very often happens, in my experience, that when they have no choice but to borrow, people in receipt of low incomes have the determination and capacity to pay back their loans over a long period of time. It is essential though that the environment in which arrangements are made are such that those who borrow know precisely what they are borrowing and what the cost will be.
In his speech, as I also mentioned, the minister commented on the nature of the sanctions imposed against those who offend against the provisions of the bill. These are severe. If I remember correctly, the fine goes up to $10,000, and imprisonment to five years. During yesterday's debate there was some discussion among certain hon. members in the course of which it was suggested that there might not be a jail in the country now which could keep anybody for five years. I know this is not the concern of the minister who is in charge of this bill but it is certainly a matter of concern to some of his colleagues, and to the general public. In any event I did point out that in considering these criminal sanctions we have to bear in mind that there are many people who are not part of any powerful financial institution, and who are not lending as a business, but who occasionally make loans to friends and relatives. These people too will have to pay attention to the law and bear in mind the complexity of its provisions, a situation which could lead to some obvious injustices, and results which no hon. member would desire. In this regard I would draw attention to clause 37 of the bill in which offences are dealt with.
We ought to be very careful when we introduce what amounts to criminal legislation in statutes which are outside the Criminal Code. One of the cardinal rules of British criminal justice is that before a person can be found guilty of a criminal offence there must have been intent, or, in the words
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors of the Latin scholars, mens rea. In other words, the person concerned must have had the intention of acting contrary to the law. Well, clause 37(1) reads as follows:
Any person who (a) stipulates for, demands, exacts or collects from a borrower a credit charge in respect of a lending transaction at a credit charge rate that exceeds the rate prescribed by the regulations for the purposes of this paragraph that was in effect on the day the transaction was entered into... is guilty of an offence and liable .. .
-liable to a fine or to imprisonment, or to both. I would point out there is nothing in this clause which requires intent to do wrong.
The minister is again with us this evening and I say to him once again that this aspect of the legislation should be considered seriously because many people who may make one loan in their whole lifetime to a son-in-law, niece or daughter, or to some other relative, will be caught by the provisions of the act and they could easily stumble into the most innocent mistakes having regard to the complexity of the measure. I believe all of us should be deeply concerned that we do not frame the sanctions in such a way as to bring fines and impose penalties for an innocent mistake on the part of someone who did not knowingly commit any offence, penalties which are not really related to any crime at all. I note, in this regard, that in the offences section, 37(b), the draftsman has gone back to the concept of fault because he says: "Any person who for the purpose of avoiding compliance with this act or the regulations . .." and so on. Here we are looking at something in the proper criminal sense and, of course, 1 have no objection to that.
On the question of the criminal aspects of the bill I would say there are about 44 clauses in it, and in about 20 of them the law will not be clear until we see the regulations which the minister proposes to promulgate at some future time. It does not take much imagination or understanding to realize that when we get into a bill which has criminal overtones and, in some cases, substantive criminal provisions, it is extremely dangerous to be passing criminal legislation in a measure which is outside the Code and where delineation of offences depends upon regulations to be passed at some future date, regulations which might well have to be changed from time to time depending upon circumstances. I raise this point not as an attack upon the bill per se but as one it would be appropriate to consider when we get into committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member a question. When he refers to 20 instances in which regulations would have to be passed he is surely not suggesting that there are 20 occasions on which offences would be prescribed?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I said that out of 44 clauses there are 20 which would require regulations and that some of those regulations will establish a situation which requires those affected by them to act in a certain way, breach of which would result in the commission of criminal offences under the act. From a question the minister was asked it does appear he is quite aware of the problem, and I am sure we will have his sympathy in committee.

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
I notice that in an early burst of honesty in his speech yesterday the minister said this legislation is long overdue. That, of course, is no argument for passing this bill in its present form. However, it is a reminder to all hon. members that the government party has been in power since 1963 and that for some reason legislation along these lines has not been introduced until now.
Before the dinner adjournment I gave some statistics showing the changing amount of credit in the commercial world in Canada. The minister made reference to another reason for bringing in the bill, and that was that the criminal or near criminal elements have, in the minister's opinion, been taking advantage of the law as it is now and as it will remain unless this bill changes it. I think it is very important that during committee hearings we have the widest ranging evidence possible on this particular aspect that the minister claims is of concern to him, as I am sure it is, as well as other matters.
The bill reaches into what is essentially a very complex part of the economic community and will have effects that probably will not become clear, in some cases, unless the people intimately connected with the day to day workings of the commercial, financial, and lending world are brought before the committee. It is my hope that the committee, with the minister's concurrence, will be generous in the matter of bringing before it the witnesses that are required. I see that the minister is nodding to indicate what seems to be, at least at this moment, general approval.
The minister and others on the government side, in the speeches which have been made so far, have said quite a lot by way of reinforcing their assumption that this bill is completely constitutional and lies entirely within the ambit of federal jurisdiction under the British North America Act. It may, Mr. Speaker, but then again it may not. Speakers for the government have emphasized that it is, Mr. Speaker, but 1 would draw to the minister's attention the fact that clause 8 of the bill seems, at least on the surface, to be in conflict with section 2 of the Ontario legislation, which is the unconscionable transactions relief act. If I remember correctly, there has been litigation on that particular statute but it has been found to be valid provincial legislation. While it is one thing to say that this bill deals with interest-although there are new words for that in the bill-and that it is clearly within federal jurisdiction, I point out the bill also deals with contracts and with the question of property and civil rights, so I put forward the caveat that this bill require some careful consideration in committee.
Clause 8 of the bill deals with the method by which the court, upon application by a borrower, determines whether or not a particular lending transaction is one for which the credit charge is warranted. In the drafting of this particular provision the court is directed to look at five particular considerations in determining whether or not the credit charge rate is warranted. This kind of legislation is unusual for what amounts to establishing what can be a criminal offence. It does not go

unnoticed that they are closed categories in that the court cannot look beyond them to something else.
I bring to the minister's attention the fact that in an ordinary real estate transaction in which there is the transfer of a deed to real property and a mortgage back, especially from a private vendor to a private purchaser, often the interest rate and terms of repayment are a factor of price. I would also say to the minister that such is the case with agreements for sale of land in some provinces, certainly in the province of British Columbia. I would ask the minister to consider that question as it will be raised in committee. Our concern here, of course, is that we must be careful not to draft legislation that restricts the court from considering every aspect that should be taken into consideration in establishing what is proper and fair.
In his speech yesterday the minister said that the object of this whole exercise, among other things was:
-to require a full, uniform and comprehensible disclosure system so that the consumer, before he enters into a deposit or borrowing transaction, will know all his rights and the obligations he will have to bear.
I think that, more than anything else, is the thrust of this legislation. However, I point out to the minister that out of 44 clauses we seem to have 20 cases that will require regulation in order to clarify the meaning of the legislation. I hope that during committee hearings the minister will agree with us that some of what he plans to place in the regulations would be appropriate to place in sections of the statute.
In his speech yesterday the minister also illustrated the effect of different interest rates on loans which apparently have the same face value. The minister took a number of examples. On a $4,000 loan with a declared rate of 12 per cent per annum, depending on deductions from the loan for various charges and other things, you could end up, Mr. Speaker, with a different interest rate. This illustration appears at page 635 of Hansard.
As his first example the minister took a loan of $4,000 with no deductions. At the end of three years the borrower would pay $4,782.96, an effective interest rate of 12.68 per cent per annum. Then the minister illustrated higher deductions from the borrowed amount. In one case there was a deduction of $50 for insurance and registration. In other case it was $250 for registration, insurance and legal fees. In yet another case it was $650 for life insurance, registration, legal fees, finder's fee and bonus.
Keeping away entirely from the aspect of provincial registration fees and other things over which a particular lender has no control, the fact of the matter is that when you get items which are deducted, such as the cost of life insurance and other things, those are of clear advantage to the borrower and it makes the example which the minister put forward a little dubious because, after all, if somebody is using part of the borrowed money to take an advantage, then of course it is going to change the interest rate on the balance outstanding after the advantage deducted has worked to the benefit of the
November 2, 1976

borrower. That is something that should be taken into consideration just so as to keep everything here in perspective.
The minister said the following in his speech yesterday, as reported at page 636 of Hansard'.
Following passage of this bill, it will be our intention to mount a comprehensive program to assist low income borrowers in the marketplace.
I do not know quite what the minister has in mind, and I think that while that does not seem to be an aspect of the provisions of the bill, it seems to be a statement of intention on the part of the minister relating to what will be government policy in his own department.
I think that before the debate is over it would be appropriate if speakers on behalf of the government enlarged a little on the bill at second reading to let us know what the government has in mind because those words can be innocuous enough until we start to find out, as we may well do, that the comprehensive program to assist low income borrowers in the market place may indeed be the structure of a whole new bureaucracy. We have no idea what this involves, and while I think that many of us have some understanding of some of the problems that the minister is concerned about in this bill, we have considerable sympathy for trying as much as is reasonable and possible to educate people not to make foolish mistakes in entering into long obligations. Nonetheless it is important that we know exactly what the minister has in mind. It may well be-I can only say this in speculation-that his department already has decided that if this bill becomes law it will be necessary to have a very extensive and quite possibly expensive counselling service across the country so that people can cope with the bill. If that indeed is the result that the minister foresees, then the bill will have to be looked at most carefully, and I invite the minister to consult with some of his colleagues and let us know before this debate is over just exactly what he has in mind.
1 want to emphasize again that this party supports this bill in principle. I think that in the remarks which all hon. members have heard from members on this side of the House concern has been expressed that the bill be efficient, effective, fair and that it works. In this spirit may I say that I hope that some of the comments that I have made tonight will be considered by my colleagues on all sides of the House, and I look forward to working with all our colleagues in committee as this bill is given more careful and appropriate examination.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: It takes time to make sense.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Even more so I wish to congratulate the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott), as well as his two predecessors, for a highly successful effort in drafting a piece of legislation which offers such comprehensive protection to the Canadian consumer in search of financial assistance. It has been some time now since this legislation was first proposed to us, but I think the end result.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors has fully justified the wait. It is clear that no effort was spared to obtain the views and assistance of experts in this field- from police authorities, to lending institutions, to the borrowers themselves. Under this legislation the borrower will be provided with the best possible protection, but at the same time without any interference in normal, legitimate financing practices.
It has been noted already in this debate that outstanding consumer credit went from $835 million in 1948 to $8.6 billion in 1967, and amounted to almost $24 billion in 1974. As this has been going on there has also been a concomitant rise in interest rates. This is as it should be; the laws of supply and demand call for it. This legislation is very timely, therefore, because as more and more people borrow money they must have an assurance that the laws of supply and demand work with them rather than against them.
Borrowers are usually very vulnerable people and are easily taken advantage of by unscrupulous lenders. The normal relationships between supply and demand can tend to be distorted therefore when a borrower needs a lender more than the lender needs the borrower. Thus every precaution must be taken to help maintain an equitable balance between these two parties. The borrowers and depositors protection bill does just that.
On the one hand this legislation provides straightforward legal sanctions against usurers and loansharks who prey on people who are often desperately short of money. On the other hand it enables the consumer to protect himself, by providing greater access to information regarding any such financial transaction. Together these dual roles will maintain the crucial balance which permits the relationship between supply and demand to work most efficiently and equitably.
I believe these two functions are of equal importance to the effectiveness of the legislation. I shall leave it to others to expand on the merits of the latter, concerning increased availability of information to the borrower. Instead I wish to focus my discussion on the specific means proposed to do away with one of the most despicable practices of our society.
This legislation is intended to replace the present concept of fixed ceilings on interest rates with three distinct rate categories: normal or "legitimate" rates; "unwarranted" rates; and "criminal" rates.
Presently the vicious business of loan sharking is, in a sense, indistinguishable from the more subtle practices of "expensive" lending firms or the entirely legitimate terms of a reputable financial institution. All are equally legal under today's inadequate usury laws-at least in so far as their monetary transactions are concerned. While the Small Loans Act, for example, sets a maximum interest rate of 24 per cent per year on loans of less than $1,500, the lender can charge any interest he wants, no matter how exorbitant, on loans above $1,500. Moreover, even when violators of the Small Loans Act are caught, the fines are too small-compared to the usual yield of the loans themselves-to provide any kind of deterrent.

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
The borrowers and depositors protection bill rectifies this incongruous situation through its differential rate structure. By establishing an "unwarranted" rate category, this legislation draws a clear distinction between legitimate interest rates on personal loans as determined in a competitive market and rates which are unnecessarily high. As the minister has explained, the "unwarranted" rate enables the borrower to take recourse against credit terms which cannot be justified by the nature of the risk involved-as in the case of especially low-risk loans-or by prevailing market conditions.
The "criminal" rate category, meanwhile, is directed specifically at loansharks and userers who run clandestine operations and who charge far more exorbitant rates than even those in the unwarranted category. Conviction for this type of offence would incur a realistically stiff penalty of up to $10,000, and two years in jail under the proposed legislation.
It has been the contention of some members of the opposition that, even with a criminal rate, the borrower is still not given adequate protection because the rate shall be set too high. To make such a claim is to ignore the need for flexibility in setting interest rates according to appropriate criteria, such as risk and duration, and to display a serious misunderstanding of the intention of the legislation as a whole. It is not a set of artificially conceived interest rates divorced from the realities of the market place, but a comprehensive, integrated program designed to bring social and economic priorities into balance. Caution must be taken not to let the criminal rate interfere with legitimately high rates. The range of legitimate rates will be made evident from the combined factors of full disclosure at the time a loan is made, the unwarranted rate range, and the new provisions for penalty-free prepayment on outstanding debts.
May I dwell for a moment, Mr. Speaker, on this last factor, the prepayment of loans? Quite simply, this provision will allow a borrower to repay any non-mortgage loan, in part or in full, before the allotted time has expired, without having to pay a penalty. This means that the borrower will only have to pay for funds for as long as he borrowed them. Here again the internal logic of the market place is reinforced as the borrower is released from unrealistic constraints and is allowed to move freely from one lender to another whenever and wherever more favourable rates can be found. This will have the inevitable effect of making the cost of borrowed money more elastic and will force lenders to police themselves so that they may keep rates down to competitive levels.
There is yet another major innovation provided in this bill which is designed to bolster the borrower's bargaining position and, thereby, provide him with more effective means to protect himself. This is the reversal of the present principle that the burden of proof rests with the borrower in loan disputes. Instead this bill would place the onus on the lender to prove that his interest charges were not unreasonable. In this fashion we can expect borrowers, who until now have had to fear
[Mr. Philbrook.J
reprisals and legal fees, to stand up and expose the usurers at whose mercy they have been for too long.
Once again, the net results can be none other than increased self-control by the lender and more reasonable rates for the borrower. With an estimated annual return of about $3 billion, loansharking has become the second largest source of income for organized crime after drug trafficking. Because the loan shark tends to prey on the poor, however, few of us realize just how big a big business it really is.
Let us look at some more startling statistics. According to revelations made at the Quebec inquiry into organized crime, 1,496 counts of shylocking were made under provincial laws and the small business loans regulations in 1973. This amounted to $3.5 million in loans and, according to inquiry officials, approximately $35 million in profits. Most startling of all, this amount was accumulated by only the 29 people who happened to be brought to justice, representing somewhere between 1 per cent and 5 per cent of the estimated total number of loan sharks operating within the Montreal area alone. This is not a very good conviction rate.
Perhaps even more dangerous to society as a whole than loansharking itself is the fact that it fosters and provokes many other forms of crime. People victimized by loan sharks can themselves be driven into criminal activity. When a borrower is terrorized with violence for defaulting on payments, he or she often chooses to push drugs, or counterfeit money, rob, or turn to prostitution; anything becomes preferable to dismemberment or death.
Along the same lines, loan sharks are a common source of funds needed for illicit purposes, such as the purchase of stolen or illegal goods, which a reputable lender would never provide. It is quite evident therefore that the effects of loansharking go well beyond the crimes perpetrated by the loan shark himself.
Just this morning on the front page of the Globe and Mail I noticed an article which speculates about the growth of yet another crime syndicate, this one in the Toronto-Hamilton area-my area where I am aware of certain concerns. What is one of their main activities? Loansharking. What are some of the consequences reported? Three deaths, an OHIP swindle amounting to about $150,000 and, most frightening of all, some curious connections with officials of the Ontario government.
If this bill does not pass with its strongly anti-loansharking provisions intact, police authorities will continue to be frustrated in their attempts to break a most vicious cycle of crime which is fueled by such activity. The loan shark will continue to prey on the most disadvantaged and those who are least capable of getting out of debt. He will continue to discount UIC cheques and welfare payments at a fraction of their cost from those who can least afford to lose them. In a more general sense, he will continue to terrorize all of us as organized crime grows into a bigger and bigger big business.
If this legislation is passed, however, we shall witness some much needed changes in the nature of borrower-lender relationships in this country. When artificial rate ceilings are
November 2, 1976

removed and the equity of competitive rates reinstated, we will have reduced much of the need for borrowers to turn to, and support, socially undesirable sources. Let me emphasize once again therefore how this bill can be expected to have far-reaching effects, not only in bringing the usurers to justice, but in reducing related crimes in other areas as well.
Neither I nor the government wish to discourage borrowing. It is an accepted way of life in the modern age, and it is generally regarded as a good and proper means of maintaining growth. Of late, however, we seem to have reached a peak in borrrowing. With interest rates steadily on the rise and the uncertainties about the furture brought on by inflation, consumer borrowing has actually begun to diminish slightly since the summer of 1975. I believe it is the responsibility of this House to assure the consumer that he can borrow money for legitimate purposes from ligitimate sources without having to worry about hidden fees, disguised costs, and perpetual indebtedness. The consumer should be allowed to borrow intelligently, so that he may feel confident to spend whenever the need arises.
Consumer spending would help the recovery this year by promising retail business and, consequently, industrial production. Consumer borrowing would contribute immensely to the recovery process as long as it is channelled properly, according to the dictates of the open market, into proper investments under equitable terms. This bill should do just that.
In closing I should like once again to congratulate the new Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and wish him well in his new career.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me first of all to say how pleased I was to hear the minister introduce Bill C-16 whose object is to give some measure of protection to borrowers and depositors. This bill is an act to, and I quote:
provide for the protection of borrowers and depositors, to regulate interest on judgment debts, to repeal the Interest Act, the Pawnbrokers Act and the Small Loans Act to amend certain other statutes in consequence thereof.
Mr. Speaker, I did say "some measure of protection" because, on reading the bill, 1 find that the government avoided attacking the root of the problem, namely excessive interest rates which are the major cause of the inflation we know today.
In introducing his bill, the minister is disconcertingly timid when he says and I quote:
I would not wish to leave the impression that Canadians are ill-served by the overwhelming majority of their lending institutions. Our banks are rightly acknowledged as some of the largest and best run in the world.
He could at least have added that they are also among the most favoured and protected in the world by their governments. If the minister is really convinced of that, why then did he ask his civil servants to think out and draft such a bill? The fact that the act has not been revised in 20 years does not necessarily make it obsolete, as the minister claims.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
If it has become obsolete, it is because of the tolerance and "laissez-faire" attitude of succeeding governments in an effort to serve, first of all, big finance. Also, the taxpayers were left completely at the mercy of loan sharks whose pecuniary appetites are never satiated. Today the government discovers that consumers are too much in debt. That discovery comes at least 20 years too late since, from 1947 to 1975, personal debts increased three times faster than personal incomes.
How can we hope, with a timid piece of legislation such as this one, to keep afloat consumers as a whole who are sumerged under this nountain eh debts? I say this bill is only a gleam of hope, which might be the last one, with which we lure the Canadian people to enable them to avoid being in the most complete deficit situation.
Let us talk a little about the interest paid on deposits and about the way to figure out this interest. 1 think not a single bank gives the same interest rate on deposits in savings accounts and the way they pay this interest is still worse. To do justice to depositors the interest should be calculated each month so that if a depositor withdraws money occasionally, this is not reflected on the interest for the other months. We must keep in mind, and the people as a whole should be well informed in this regard, that these savings accounts of the workers build up the reserves of chartered banks. According to the Bank Act, the banks have the power to increase the value of these savings five times and to lend the total at an 11 and even 12 per cent interest rate.
In brief, if the bank agrees to open a savings account for a depositor, every $100 deposit he makes allows the bank to lend $1,500 at 10 or 11 per cent, and even at a higher rate sometimes, to a potential lender. In other words, the bank will pay the depositor $8 in interest while on that same $100 it will be able to get up to $160 in interest. So every $8 spent in interest by the chartered banks brings in $160. And then the banks tell us that money is expensive for them. Worse still, these same banks try by every possible means to reduce the depositor's interest. Therefore, I say that in addition to proposing a uniform interest formula, this bill should also provide that interest in the accounts-being in fact the bank's legal reserve-be paid each month.
Let us come back now to the lenders who have been given free way over the last few years. What else could be expected when the example came from the top? Everybody remembers that when the Bank Act was last amended the Liberal government removed the interest ceiling for chartered banks. Chartered banks-the most important institutions in Canada-are now allowed to ask any interest rate they want simply because the government has suppressed the interest rate ceiling. And after such an aberration, we wonder about the inflation rate.
Mr. Speaker, I said it time and again in this House that inflation started when the government removed all restraints to banking operations. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, that when a bank is permitted to charge rates of 10 and even 12 per cent, no lending institution will likely operate below that level. I do not say that I agree with excessive rates practiced by some private lenders but I suggest that we should start from the
80001 -45

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors beginning. Let us take the bull by the horns instead of trying to hold it back by the tail.
This is why I was saying at the outset that this government was afraid of coming to grips with this problem. It is constantly trying to evade the issue, making people believe that one day-not today and not tomorrow either-the government is going to be logical and tackle the real problems facing the workers. Meanwhile, through Bill C-16 it will try to cool off the small lenders who, as we all know, are taking unfair advantage of the consumers.
Bill C-16, dealing with prepayments, has a clause according to which a borrower who wants to make a prepayment is not liable to any penalty when he comes to pay the total amount outstanding under the transaction. For example, say a finance company makes a loan repayable over 36 months, and the borrower finds a way to pay back within 10 or 12 months. Why should the borrower have to pay interest for 36 months or even for 5 or 6 months more only because he wants to get rid of his debt? We should not forget, Mr. Speaker, that when the lending institution gets full prepayment from the borrower, it can lend this very amount on the following day and for months get double interest on the same loan. And the government was well aware of these legal thefts. Why did it tolerate them? The other governments were also aware of them. Why have they tolerated them during the last twenty years?
Another sad situation, like the minister indicated, is the widespread practice in Canada of lending money on welfare cheques or tax refunds. This practice is quite widespread in areas of high unemployment and welfare. It is very natural for a family man who has four or five children to feed and who has to wait for his unemployment cheque for one and maybe two or three months to try to find some money somewhere. This is quite natural. He must find money to feed his family. When a man who is unemployed comes to see me and I read on his benefit card "Case under study", I know that the situation is serious, Mr. Speaker. For weeks and weeks it is written on top of his card "Case under study". I wonder if the minister, who gives overly strict orders to his officials when he demands lengthy investigations like those that are still being carried out for forest workers, is well aware of the damage that he is doing to these family men.
I have just learned that in a case which has come up in the last few days, a delay of eight to ten weeks in the payment of benefits was caused by the fact that the official must enquire personally from each forestry employer to ensure that the beneficiary is really entitled to the stamps. Mr. Speaker, nothing could be more ridiculous. We shall soon need an army to go through forestry sites to check if such or such a forestry worker is entitled to unemployment insurance. This is shocking! That is why forestry workers must go to pawnbrokers to whom they will sometimes give up to one third of their benefits to feed their family. Who must we blame, Mr. Speaker, in such circumstances?
Before putting the blame on lenders, I must put the blame on the minister because of his restrictive laws whose impact is amplified by regulations which are even more restrictive. Thus,
[Mr. Gauthier (Roberval).J
we can wonder if the Unemployment Insurance Act was not made in the first place for civil servants so that the greatest number of people could work in the civil service. Sometimes you feel that the unemployed is considered a criminal because he cannot find a job. His family will be left to vegetate and his children will be in danger of getting ill. I could give similar examples about welfare recipients who are obliged to call upon such lenders as are mentioned in Bill C-16. In the case of income tax refunds, the situation is also quite bad. Some people are waiting for their income tax refund cheque and must borrow money to pay their debts.
Mr. Speaker, I cannot understand why a responsible government cannot take the necessary measures so that everything could be done in time. However, we feel that the number of employees is quite sufficient. To my mind, they are so numerous that they create a state of confusion and quite often the cheques are lost because we have too many civil servants.
To sum up, I would say that all these cases are due to bad management by the departments concerned. These lenders could not survive if the government could better understand the social problems and if it were more conscious of its responsibilities. Finally, I would like to come back to the subject of mortgage loans. I wonder why the minister makes a difference between ordinary loans and mortgage loans when it comes to prepayments. I cannot understand why insurance companies or other lending institutions that grant mortgage loans would punish a borrower who wants to repay his loan.
Maybe somebody will tell me that it is because the lending company had to make a contract or raise mortgages, but we should not forget that it is the borrower who pays, it is not the company, all the costs are to the borrower. I could understand the situation if the lending insurance company had to respect the original interest rate. But, every five years, the companies have the right to increase their interest rates so that a loan granted at a rate of 6 or 7 per cent a few years ago can reach an interest rate of 10 to 12 per cent according to the whims of the lending companies.
And this is done with the blessings of our governments. The ony apology the minister gives us for his apathy is that, because of the particular nature of mortgages and of the mortgage market, he can do nothing but accept the present situation. Did anybody take into consideration the excessive profits of insurance companies? Did anybody wonder where these companies took the money to build their huge skyscrapers? From the pockets of those who will be all their lives the victims of those companies.
Those lending companies cling to their customers as leeches cling to their victims. They set insurance premiums, the amounts of municipal rates, school, taxes and all through the year they collect them and hand them over at the very end of the year and often two months late. What do they do with the money they collect each month? They lend it for 12 months and draw the interests and thus all those interests are added to the interests levied on mortgages. The government does not want to legislate in those fields. Is it an accomplice or does it merely ignore what is going on?
November 2, 1976

Mr. Speaker, we approve Bill C-16 and hope it will be referred to the committee of the whole to make the necessary amendments and make it more acceptable and more effective for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REGULATE INTEREST ON JUDGMENT DEBTS AND AMEND CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Bill helps carry out, with certain important exceptions which I shall mention shortly, the key plank in the election platform on which the Liberal party fought and won the election of July, 1974. The fact that the bill came some 2Vi years after that election makes it no less welcome. It represents a long overdue and greatly needed reform and updating of federal law dealing with consumer credit.
I am pleased to see the bill since the carrying out of such a reform and updating of federal consumer law was an initiative I announced as minister before the 1974 election, and work on this was under way as the campaign began.
The bill has many desirable features. For example, two were stated in the 1974 election platform in these terms: "Legislation requiring disclosure of the effective rate of interest in all interest-bearing transactions" and, "Legislation allowing the buyer to pay off residential mortgages during the first five years of the agreement without excessive penalties." However, the many desirable features of the bill were outlined by the minister is his speech opening the debate on second reading, as well as in the material he released at the time the bill was first tabled in the House a few days ago. Therefore I do not intend to state them all again at this time. However, I do want to make some comments and raise some questions about some of the things that are in the bill and, more important, about some of the things that are not.
My purpose is a constructive one. My aim is to help ensure that by the time it is adopted the bill is the best one possible and, therefore, the kind of legislation that Canadian consumers are entitled to get from their federal government. In spite of all the good features of the legislation I do not think a case has been sufficiently made as yet that it is already at this level of achievement.
It is good to know that the bill will require a lender to inform a consumer of the true total cost of a loan and that the lender must include it in the total credit charge. However, the question remains as to whether the bill deals in the best way with the problem of excessive credit charges, of excessive interest rates. The bill proposes the repeal of the Small Loans Act with its ceiling on interest rates charged on loans of less than $1,500. In its place it proposes that there be what in effect is a maximum permissible ceiling set by regulation-the criminal rate of interest-and that any rate below this is acceptable unless a court rules it is unwarranted. The minister has not yet said what this criminal rate will be. I gather it is intended to be very high. I understand that a rate of at least 70 per cent per annum is being contemplated.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
