All this means that the only recourse a consumer will have if he is charged a rate which is high but below the very high criminal rate is to ask a court to rule that it is unwarranted, or not to pay it and wait until he is sued, at which time the lender will have to prove that the rate is not unwarranted.
The act also says that the borrower can pay off the loan at any time, assuming of course that he is able to find the necessary funds at a lower rate. However, this latter opportunity also has its limitations and problems which I will refer to in a moment. Frankly I do not think that it is totally realistic to expect the average consumer-borrower who does not like the rate he is being charged for a transaction to have recourse to the courts as his basic form of relief. We are talking about people who, in many cases, are of low income, of limited education, and who are hesitant and unsure of themselves when it comes to dealing with large organizations, whether they be business or government. They find, as do most Canadians, our court system to be forbidding and unknown territory which is difficult and costly to enter or to leave. The bill does nothing to remove these legitimate kinds of concerns.
The borrower can apply to a court to review the transaction and to ask that the credit charge be declared unwarranted. But to what court can he apply? According to the bill it will not be to a small claims court with its relative lack of paper work, formality and cost. Instead he will have to apply to a county court or some other superior court, with all this means in terms of red tape, formality and expense, including the practical necessity of having a lawyer.
The borrower can cease his payments and wait until he is sued for payment, hoping that the court will say the lender has not discharged the onus the bill will put on him to prove the rate is unwarranted. However, the borrower will them have the often frightening experience of being served legal papers and going into the unfamiliar environment of the court system, with the cost of legal representation and so on.
The burden of proof, the onus, may be on the lender to prove the rate is warranted. However, this does not mean that the burden can never be discharged by the lender and that the court will always, or even generally, find in favour of the borrower and will declare the rate to be unwarranted and, therefore, not payable. The proceedings in question will be civil and not criminal in nature. This means the lender will not have to prove his case beyond a reasonable doubt, as he would in a criminal case if the onus of proof were on his shoulders. The benefit of any doubt will not, therefore, have to be given to the borrower, as has to be done for the defendant in a criminal case. All the lender has to do is to prove his case, as the bill says, "to the satisfaction of the court," which I presume means discharging the burden of proof in civil cases, proving his point on a balance of the probabilities and in the light of the factors set out in the bill in this regard.
It may well be that the judges will not find it difficult in many cases to do this after looking at such factors as "the cost
80001 -451/2

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors of funds to the lender at and about the time the lending transaction was entered into;" "other costs to the lender of doing business that are reasonable having regard to the nature and scale of business of the lender;" and, "the degree of risk assumed by the lender having regard to the nature and value of any security provided, and the age, business capacity, financial position and mental and physical health of the borrower", and they will find the lender has proved his point.
The protection the bill promises the unwarranted charge concept will bring may well prove to be an illusion for many borrowers once it becomes law, especially those who now benefit from the maximum ceiling rates under the Small Loans Act for loans under $1,500. The minister in the speech in which he opened this debate talked about the limited protection now given by the Small Loans Act, pointing out that it does not apply to loans over $1,500. He pointed out as well that the total amount of loans made under the ceiling has been steadily declining in recent years. This may well be generally true. However, there are still very substantial numbers of people obtaining loans under the $1,500 ceiling and therefore benefiting from the approach of the existing Small Loans Act.
The latest report of the Superintendent of Insurance on the operations of small loans companies and money lenders licensed under the Small Loans Act is for the year ending December 31, 1974. The report states that in 1974 there were $412,204,415 in loans made under the $1,500 ceiling involving a total of 647,739 accounts. The minister said in his speech that only $296 million was lent in 1974 under the Small Loans Act ceiling. This does not appear correct from my reading of the 1974 report. Perhaps he will explain this discrepancy when he winds up the debate.
What will happen to the more than half a million people who apparently have been benefiting from the step rate and ceilings approach of the Small Loans Act, if this bill is passed in its present form? They will be left to what may turn out to be the illusory protection of the unwarranted rate concept with which the government proposes to replace what presently exists. We have had something like the unwarranted rate concept in the unconscionable transactions relief acts that have been in place for many years in most if not all of the provinces. The fact is, however, that they have been rarely used by consumer borrowers and, when used, rarely found beneficial by them. Also, what is to prevent a lender or a group of lenders from having an informal black list of people who have gone to court to complain that a credit charge is unwarranted? Will someone who asks a court to declare a credit charge unwarranted ever be able to get a loan again from the lender in question, or any lender? The bill does not deal with this particular problem that could be created by the unwarranted rate concept it proposes.
I think it is somewhat unreal and impractical to expect most borrowers faced with excessive credit charges to go on their own to the courts in order to take advantage of the new provisions in the bill, supposedly for their greater protection. In the bill the government is not proposing any mechanism of

its own to initiate and present applications for relief on behalf of borrowers, not is the government proposing to help pay the cost of such court action where a borrower goes to court on his own. Also the government is not proposing any mechanism of its own to defend the borrower or help the borrower bear the cost of defence where the borrower is taken to court for refusing to pay unwarranted credit charges.
To be meaningful, the unwarranted rate concept must require the administrator appointed under the act and his staff to act on behalf, at the very least, of low-income borrowers, to bring action on their behalf before the courts or to defend actions for the purpose of having the court rule the credit charge in question unwarranted. In any event, the minister has not in my view as yet sufficiently made the case for the total abandonment of the step rate ceiling approach of the present Small Loans Act. The fact that the $1,500 ceiling and the rates set out in the act may be out-of-date does not mean the concept as a whole should be totally abandoned. Instead this is simply an argument for raising the ceiling and providing a new formula for setting acceptable interest rates.
The Royal Commission on Banking and Finance, the Porter Commission, did not propose removing the ceiling. The special joint committee of the Senate and House on Consumer Credit-The Croll-Basford Committee-did not recommend removing the ceiling. Instead after careful study they both recommended raising it to a more appropriate level-which at the time of their reports they said should be $5,000 rather than $1,500-and also modifying the allowable rates of interest.
One co-chairman of that special committee is now our distinguished and capable Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford) in this government which has presented the bill we are now debating. It seems to me that the point of view of his famous report on consumer credit, on the desirability of the ceiling system for small loans, still has validity today.
Also let us look at the Liberal election platform of 1974. This platform did not propose removing that ceiling. The Consumers Association of Canada now has urged that the maximum rate and ceiling concept of the Small Loans Act be maintained. Proposals in this bill to eliminate that approach must be carefully examined to see if they will, in fact, achieve the objectives claimed for them of providing greater access to credit at more reasonable rates for borrowers, while providing them with easy access for relief if they accept unwarranted rates.
However, this bill does nothing to ensure that the low income borrower who has in the past found it difficult to obtain credit from legitimate institutions, will not continue to be forced into the hands of loan sharks rather than getting that credit from legitimate lenders. The bill does nothing to ensure that the borrower, who found it difficult in the past to get credit except from companies licensed under the Small Loans Act, will, when this bill is passed, get credit on terms as favourable as those now provided for loans under the act, either from small loan companies or other credit granting
November 2, 1976

institutions. The minister in his speech on second reading said at one point:
That is why we propose the repeal of the Small Loans Act. Instead we are proposing a strong and comprehensive set of protective devices applicable to all forms and levels of consumer credit so that consumers will be assured of access to loans bearing fair and reasonable credit charges.
At another point in that same speech he said:
-I would remind the House of the prepayment privilege and the unwarranted rate provision. A low income borrower who is a good risk-and many of them are-is entitled to get a rate that takes that fact into account. His credit rating may be as good and perhaps better than that of higher income people, but because he is ill-informed, timid, or a person alarmed by forms, he will tend to avoid institutions which will gladly deal with him. Now this borrower can go freely to any institution, obtain a loan at rates commensurate with his true credit risk, and prepay the higher rate loan he is carrying.
However, in spite of the impression conveyed by these words, if the bill simply is passed in its present form, no lender will be obliged to make any loan he is not obliged to make now, and lenders have never been obliged to make loans. No borrower will have any greater right to obtain credit, to obtain a loan, after the bill is passed than he has at present.
The bill adds nothing by way of any absolute assurance that individual consumer borrowers, who consider themselves sufficiently credit worthy to obtain loans at reasonable rates, will ever get them. In fact totally absent from the bill is a pledge made quite explicitly in the 1974 Liberal election platform which said:
The Liberal policy includes .. . plan for a low-income insurance plan to help establish credit for low-income, steadily employed wage earners.
We need explanations as to why the program promised in the 1974 election platform is not in the bill right now. We should have the government's commitment, before the bill finally becomes law, to the early creation of such a program. If this program comes in the form of federal government guarantees against loss for loans made by financial institutions to low-income, steadily employed borrowers, there would be no valid argument that such a program would be too costly to the public treasury. However, such a program would help fill a need the bill really does not deal with adequately.
The minister's second reading speech said:
In placing this bill before the House, I would not wish to leave the impression that Canadians are ill-served by the overwhelming majority of their lending institutions.
I suppose it is generally correct that these institutions are of good quality in comparison to much of the rest of the world and that they do provide adequately for the needs of many Canadians. But having said this, the question remains, if it is true as the minister says in his speech that the "police estimate that loan sharking has become a $3 billion a year business in Canada" why should this be the case? Why should a business of this size have developed? If our lending institutions are doing as good a job as the minister says, why do so many Canadians feel that they must turn to loan sharks in order to fill their needs for credit? Why do so many apparently feel that loan sharks are more accessible than our much vaunted financial institutions? Neither the bill nor the minister's speech gives us any real answer to these key questions.
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
However, the high degree of recourse by consumer-borrowers to loan sharks as described by the minister leads to the conclusions, in my view at least, that there is something necessary in the field of consumer credit that our legitimate financial institutions are not doing. There is a gap they are not filling. To fill this gap calls for early co-operative action both by financial institutions and the government, with the government showing leadership in filling the need of low-income borrowers. This involves not only a special lending program of the type outlined in the election platform but also a new, wide-ranging program for consumer education on the wise use and choice of credit. Such a program has not yet been proposed either in the bill or in the minister's speech on behalf of the government.
An aim of the bill is to enable strong action to be taken against loan sharks. The criminal rate concept, the requirements for record keeping, prohibition against oppressive treatment and harassment of borrowers will all be helpful for this purpose. However, something is missing from the bill which is very important when it comes to dealing with loan sharks. It is something which is also very important for dealing with lenders who do not exactly fall in the loan shark category but whose practices can be described as questionable if not as being downright unscrupulous.
What is missing from the bill is the concept of licensing. The 1974 Liberal election platform promised:
-legislation requiring federal registration of all money lenders not already registered who lend to individuals.
Not only has this promise not been carried out in the bill but the bill actually proposes the elimination of those requirements already in our law for the licensing of small loans companies and money lenders as defined in the Small Loans Act. No explanation has been given, not only for the seeming abandonment of that 1974 election pledge, but also of the licensing provisions we already have. Licensing procedures can be an effective way of ensuring that those subject to them meet the standards of the law with regard to acceptable conduct in the market place. They can be used to remove from the market place entirely those who have shown through their past conduct that they do not deserve to be there at all. A licensing system provides a basis for cease and desist proceedings and voluntary compliance proceedings that can be quicker and more effective in many instances than having recourse solely to prosecutions which often result only in monetary penalties against the lender with no meaningful direct redress for borrowers.
The bill before us would not prevent anyone from continuing to make loans using questionable or unscrupulous techniques, no matter how many times such a lender were to be convicted under the act or how many times the court ruled the credit charges extracted by that lender to be unwarranted. As long as the lender could find enough unwary customers, it could stay in business.

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
A licensing procedure authorizing a tribunal to order the removal of the licence after a fair hearing and with rights of appeal could deal effectively with this kind of bad actor in the market place. The proposed law will not only allow them to continue operating, it even removes from the sanction and scrutiny of a licensing procedure those firms now obliged to subject themselves to it under the present Small Loans Act. The lack of a licensing procedure should at the very least, be explained and justified by the government during the course of consideration of this bill.
A simple approach would be to require the licensing, the registration, of all moneylenders not subject to be licensed under other federal or provincial laws. One can agree that duplication of licensing is not necessary. But why remove even the requirement for licensing from those now subject to it under the existing law? Whatever may be said for the authority to be given to the new administrator under the act, that authority is not to exercise a licensing jurisdiction.
The bill gives those harmed through infractions of it the right to sue for civil damages. This is a step in the right direction, but its value is limited. There is the whole problem of access to the courts as discussed earlier. Also, the cost of going to court may not be worth while, even though the interest as a percentage of the loan is very high, if the loan itself is small. The bill provides no right, as it should, for borrowers similarly harmed by a lender or group of lenders to band together through a class action to achieve relief through the courts, something which might not be worth while for them to do alone. The bill also makes no provision for the administrator to take action for damages even on behalf of individual low income borrowers.
In looking at the unwarranted rate concept, it should be noted that a decision by a court that a rate is unwarranted applies only to the case which is brought before it-to the one transaction for which a review is sought. Certainly the same judge, or another, may use such a ruling as a precedent when considering another case. However, a decision that a rate is unwarranted will not be binding on lenders with respect to any other transaction even though such other transaction may contain identical terms. Further individual court actions would have to be undertaken.
Therefore it could well be that the fear of having their credit charges challenged in court as being unwarranted might not have the salutary and self-policing effect hoped for by the government and expressed in the minister's speech. Instead, some lenders might rely on their understanding of the law of averages, expecting that while some of their loans might be challenged as unwarranted, most would not be challenged, for the reasons I have already outlined. Some lenders might well decide to take their chances in the expectation that while a few of their loans and credit charges would be struck down by the courts, any loss involved would be more than made up by excessive and unjustified gains from charging rates which might be unwarranted but which would never be looked at by any court, no matter what the bill in its present form may say.

Finally, Mr. Speaker, much of the effectiveness of the act will come not from what is said in the bill itself but rather in regulations, the contents of which have not yet been disclosed to us. There are more than 20 places in the bill where matters are left to be defined and made meaningful by regulation.
I would also point out that the bill would allow even those beneficial features it contains to be made meaningless-to be withdrawn-since, according to clause 31 (l)(a) the government may make regulations "exempting any class of lending transactions from the application of this act or of any provision or provisions of this act". In some cases regulations can be made excluding whole classes of institutions from the provisions of the bill. I recognize that delegation to the government by parliament of the right to make and change definitions and details of the application of a law by regulation helps keep that law relevant in the light of changing practices in the market place, but it can also mean that this bill, after it is debated and voted upon, may later turn out to be far different both in form and application from what it is now, before the regulations are finally issued.
The bill does say that before any regulations made under it may be proclaimed in force there must be a reasonable time left to comment on them. That is, no doubt, worth while for groups and individuals in the private sector. But as far as parliament is concerned it cannot be a substitute for knowing the government's exact intentions on the important matters the bill proposes be left to be spelled out in regulations.

My comments and questions have been raised in a constructive way with the aim of securing the best possible legislation for Canadian consumers. This is extremely important since, as has been pointed out, consumer debt has increased from $1 billion in 1947 to $23 billion at the present time and has come to represent 22 per cent of the total disposable income of Canadians. The importance of consumer credit is so great that, to use the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he announced the consumer credit plank in the 1974 Liberal election platform, "We feel it is vital to provide the utmost in protection and equity in the field of consumer credit." I believe the bill deserves support on second reading, but in allowing it to pass through the balance of the parliamentary process we must make sure that it does, in fact, provide "the utmost in protection and equity in the field of consumer credit".
Finally, Mr. Speaker, however much, in the words of Edward Fitzgerald in his "Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam", one would like to "take the cash and let the credit go", the economy we have now, and which we are likely to have in the foreseeable future, does not make this possibility at all likely. Our duty, therefore, is to ensure that credit goes with, and not against, the best interests of all Canadians.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to make my comments on Bill C-16 1 might be excused for feeling a little pity for the minister. It seems that in his new post he has not had a chance to get agreement from all members of his party over there. It is not often that I have to wait when 1 get up for applause for a member on the government side to die down.
I find it very strange, Mr. Speaker, in fact incredible, that a government that has allowed such high inflation as we have been experiencing in past years should be so worried, as it is now, about high interest rates. While being concerned with high interest rates we find that it has removed the ceiling on interest rates and replaced those ceilings with some unknown rates, to be included in some regulation to be promulgated at some unknown time.
1 listened to the minister telling us about his consultations. It is true that there were consultations, Mr. Speaker, but consultation to be meaningful has to be two way. 1 should like to refer to a letter from the Consumers Association of Canada in which they make reference to discussions with the minister held by several representatives from their association. I think it is significant that this letter is dated October 20, exactly one week before this bill was introduced by the minister in this House.
In their letter the Consumers Association of Canada make reference to several proposals that they want the minister to consider in drafting the legislation. The first matter they refer to is the ceilings. They favour retention of a graduated ceiling
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors on the cost of loans up to $7,500. They are also concerned that ceilings should be set at levels that realistically reflect the cost of lending money. With reference to the unwarranted rate, the Consumers Association has this to say:
We do not believe that the proposed provision involving an unwarranted rate concept and a seven times prime rate ceiling are adequate substitutes for explicit regulation of small loan rates.
Small loan rates have not been mentioned in any way in any of the material put out or in the ministers own remarks in this House. Apparently, judging from this letter, there was a discussion with the CAC and the minister about a rate, and presumably a seven times prime rate ceiling was mentioned by one side or the other. The prime rate in Canada today is 1114 per cent, so if we are to have an unwarranted rate seven times that, it does not take very long to calculate that this comes to 77 and some odd per cent interest, or nearly 80 per cent, as one hon. member has already mentioned tonight.
That may sound like a very high figure and the minister has not given us any idea what he plans to do in connection with the ceiling. It might be worth reflecting that the Small Loans Act, which will be repealed if this bill is passed, provided for a nominal rate of 24 per cent per annum. This act was last amended 20 years ago, in 1956, and I suspect that 24 per cent per annum in 1956 was roughly six times the likely prime rate at that time of approximately 4 per cent.
The Consumers Association goes on to suggest that the unwarranted rate system depends ultimately on the ability and willingness of those most likely to need protection to go to court. I will be saying something more about that in a few minuter, Mr. Speaker.
Another concern of the Consumers Association is disadvantaged borrowers. They express concern about the loan sharking problem and therefore favour inclusion of an absolute ceiling for legal interest rates. There is reference somewhere in the material to a criminal rate, but I have not been able to find the term "criminal rate" in the bill and certainly it does not seem to be defined there.
In discussing disadvantaged borrowers the Consumers Association says this:
In any case, the widespread vulnerability of low-income populations to credit difficulties is by now well known, and should therefore be made a priority target of government policy and program development.
The CAC also favours retention of licensing requirements for regulated lenders, subject to exemption of lenders already governed by existing or future federal or provincial licensing requirements. As we have heard from others in this debate, Mr. Speaker, the licensing requirements will have disappeared with the passage of this legislation.
Some of the other concerns mentioned by the CAC in its letter to the minister are civil sanctions; the definition of "credit transaction", which has not been clarified, Mr. Speaker; non-purchase money mortgages, to which they would like to see attached the right of prepayment without penalty; and finally in the field of federal provincial relations they recommend regular consultation between federal and provincial governments.	.

November 2, 1976
Protection of Borrowers and Depositors
What makes this letter all the more incredible, Mr. Speaker, is its final sentence to the minister, as follows:
I trust that you will be giving close attention to our views before introducing the new bill to parliament.
We know that hardly was the letter received by the minister that the bill was presented to parliament. One can only guess that the reason for the sudden introduction of this bill was the government's failure to have anything else of any meaning on the docket of this House.
To underline the disappointment of the Consumers Association of Canada at the ignoring of their recommendations, 1 should like to refer to their bulletin which is dated the day after the bill was introduced into this House. They have this to say:
It is clear that comprehensive credit legislation to deal with all types of credit transactions is long overdue ... And we warmly welcome those elements of the new bill which will help to provide greater protection to consumers who borrow and lend money.
They then express some severe reservations, such as the government's proposal to eliminate the limits on interest rates on small loans. They hope that these features will be amended when the bill is debated in parliament. They also consider that the bill allows consumers only limited means to obtain restitution for losses incurred as a result of illicit lending practices. They also make reference to the fact that this is a long and complicated bill.
This important group, the Consumers Association of Canada, is funded by this government in order to bring some ground level reports forward from the consumers of this country, who are the very people that the minister is proposing to help. There is no evidence that he has received any support from the very people at whom he has aimed this legislation.
As speakers on this side of the House have already said, we are in general agreement with the stated aims of this bill. In particular, the minister said that he wanted to protect Canadian borrowers. We could not agree with anything more. Secondly, the minister says he wants to provide more and better information on credit, which is another commendable and long overdue aim with which we totally agree. Further, he wants to eliminate unnecessary complexities and confusion in credit dealings, again extremely commendable, Mr. Speaker. He also wants to define uniform rules to protect borrowers and depositors. That also is fine. We have four important principles with which we are in total agreement.
These aims are given priority in the bill because consumer borrowing has increased at such a high rate, even considering the rates of inflation that have had to be overcome. For example, in 1950 the consumer credit figure given is SI.2 billion, or 10 per cent of personal expenditures. By 1974 consumer credit had reached $20.6 billion and amounted to 26 per cent of personal expenditures in that year. That did not include money borrowed on mortgages on individual houses and condominiums, which money was actually used not for the purchase of the real property but for the purchase of consumer goods. But frequently to borrow on a mortgage on a house is a cheaper way of borrowing than by the conventional financing
[Mr. Clarke (Vancouver Quadra).J
methods. On average, statistics show that every employed member of the labour force owed $2,250 in 1974.
Despite this dramatic change the Small Loans Act and the Interest Act have not been altered significantly, since 1956 in the case of the Small Loans Act and since 1917 in the case of the Interest Act. These bills remained substantially the same in spite of the Porter Commission of 1964 and the report on consumer credit in 1967 which showed the need for change. In 1975, just about one year ago, the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs said in a speech that there has been serious need for change for a long time.
There has obviously been a lot of thought in the past and it is nice to see that the government is taking steps to make some corrections. One could wonder whom one could blame for all this delay. It is interesting to note that since I was two years old we have had less than six years of non-Liberal government in this country. In other words, for 35 of the last 41 years we have had Liberal governments.

I should add that it is likely to change very soon. I do not see how hon. members opposite can sit there and applaud the performance of this government.
1 want to deal with some of the complaints of a general nature which we might have in connection with this bill. First of all we find that the borrower is defined as a person or a closely held corporation with fewer than 15 shareholders. However, when we come to the mortgage clauses of this act, namely clauses 14 and 15, the definition of "borrower" is changed to exclude a closely held corporation. Many individuals band together to form corporations, for business dealings or whatever, and sometimes individuals have corporations and the home is owned by a corporation. These individuals will now be denied the rights given to individual borrowers.
The minister has made a big point about the right to pay-eff by individual borrowers, but all he has done under the new rules is to allow a complete pay-off of a mortgage after three years instead of five years. The individual borrower always had the right to pay off his loan in full after five years. There has been no change in the penalty payment required in paying off an individual's mortgage-it is still three months.
Another specific type of complaint is found in Clause 31 and it covers the regulations. It is stated that the governor in council may make regulations. We have heard about how many different times the regulations have been referred to in the bill, and 1 will not try to detail them all, but there are some glaring examples-about six here, I think-in clause 6, with regard to the form prescribed by the regulation, that the information must be filed in a form to be prescribed by the regulations, and the contents must be such information as is
November 2, 1976

prescribed by the regulations. That has regard to the relevant credit charge.
Clause 7 requires that the lender shall, in a manner and form prescribed, disclose to the borrower such information as is prescribed by the regulations. Here we are again asked to approve a bill which does not tell us the form or how the information should be filed, and it does not say what information is required to be filed. We wonder how one can comply with a statute that does not contain these details and how we can be asked to pass such a bill. In clause 18 we are told of the manner of providing statements to borrowers and that the fee prescribed is to be determined by regulation.
Clause 20 refers to the content of advertisements for deposit taking institutions which is to be set out by regulation. Clause 21 refers to regulations for a class of institution excepted from the bill, and the calculations must be in the manner prescribed by the regulations as well as the intervals which are to be prescribed by the regulations. Finally under clause 31 we find that the governor in council may exempt any class of lending transactions from the act.
There are so many holes there that one really does not know what kind of thing we are asked to pass. We have a bill with unspecified maximums and an unspecified criminal rate of interest. We find that the borrower has to take after-the-fact action which is really quite ineffective, too indefinite, and nobody knows where he stands on various transactions.
The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) commented on the problems a borrower might find if he has to go to court. The bill is absolutely silent on legal costs, and I imagine there would be very few borrowers who would be willing to take a chance in a court on further burdening themselves with high legal costs as well as interest rates they have been called upon to pay. I think the hon. member for Windsor West made the problem quite clear with regard to the average small borrower and his dealings with the courts. When we had the small loans provisions, the 24 per cent was spelled out in the act and it worked well for the few years it had before it was finally repealed. Even then the ceiling was $1,500, and all that did was to encourage the people who were unwilling to get involved with the small loans regulations to increase the amount of their loans to over $1,500. The figure often seen was $1,525. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

AIRPORTS-VANCOUVER INTERNATIONAL-SUGGESTED ENVIRONMENTAL STUDIES IN CONNECTION WITH PROPOSED THIRD RUNWAY-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes that 1 have available I want to remind all hon. members that early in 1973 questions were raised in the House by members of this party, myself included, concerning a proposed expansion of Vancouver Airport which consisted primarily of the building of a new runway which would be closer by a considerable distance to the heavily built up portion of Vancouver and which would extend into the estuary part of the Fraser River, which is an important salmon resting area for young fish having come down the Fraser River and before going into the Pacific Ocean. The two immediate problems were pollution, first of the water, and the second of noise for those people affected by the new runway. There are the other problems of how this would affect the entire area.
Eventually the government of the day agreed to establish an airport planning committee to study this entire issue. That was established early in 1973 and the report came down in March, 1976. The result of the deliberations of that planning committee, which included members of the Vancouver regional government, interested people in the aviation industry, the Department of Public Works, the Department of Transport, the Department of the Environment, the Department of Urban Affairs, The Community Forum, the City of Vancouver and the greater Vancouver regional district, was that there was a split decision, but the majority was for not proceeding with the airport expansion because a case had not been made for it by the Ministry of Transport. The issue was whether or not a long runway, which would extend into the estuary, should be built.
Subsequent to the report of the airport planning committee the then minister of the environment said that perhaps we could have a shorter runway which would not extend into the estuary. On March 7, 1976, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) issued a press release in which he said:
710

November 2, 1976
Adjournment Debate
A federal government decision is expected to be made within the next few months and all interested parties are asked to present their views to the minister as soon as possible.
In the press release the minister did not set out what kind of a proposal was now being looked at, but it became very clear that the minister had decided to take the decision making from the airport planning committee and make his own decision in the secrecy of his own office as to whether or not, first of all, there ought to be any new runway, and second, what kind of runway it ought to be. Subsequently in the House the minister was asked on several occasions in recent weeks just what was going on.
On October 25, as reported at page 402 of Hansard I asked the minister if he would advise the House at what stage were the deliberations concerning the so-called third runway at Vancouver International Airport. The minister replied that some further studies of an environmental nature were seen as necessary before any final decision was taken. Then the minister went on to say a most extraordinary thing. He said that in the meantime a certain amount of regular fill that is available without impact upon the waters nearby is being obtained and arranged for pre-loading in the runway area.
I asked the minister if this meant that the decision had in fact been made to go ahead with the new runway and he said no, that it did not mean that. Then on November 1 I asked the minister again if he could tell us what was happening with regard to the situation, especially in view of the fact that an environmental panel had been selected in July this year but had apparently been disbanded. The minister did not know what the reference to that environment panel was and said:
My view is that the panel that is to be, is still to be and there will be an announcement on that in due course.
It is extraordinary that on September 18 a member of his department spoke to the citizens' group in Vancouver and answered certain questions. He was asked whether an environmental panel had been established and was asked the date and formation of the original panel. He answered that that was in July of this year. He was asked this question:
Was there actually a specified membership of persons on the panel?
He answered:
Yes there was a list drawn up and a panel meeting actually was held, as a first go-around to inform the panel members what it was all about.
He then went on to say that the panel was disbanded and has no longer any standing.
There are certain questions which arise out of this. The events are well known in the city of Vancouver, British Columbia, and there are certain questions which demand answers. First, why has the minister circumvented the planning and review process established three years ago under the airport planning committee which involved the federal government, the local government, the greater Vancouver regional district, the city of Vancouver, and the citizens of the affected area? The second question is what happened to the representations, if any, which the minister invited from the public in his press release of March 12, 1976? Are we ever going to see them?
The third question is just how could anyone comment on a proposal when no details of the proposal-or proposals-have ever been given to anyone? In other words, we have no details as to what it is the minister is in fact studying. The fourth question is why did the minister say in his press release of March 12, that, and I quote, "a decision would be made in the next few months"? It is now eight months later, and all is confusion.
The next question is why has the minister refused, since March, 1976, up to now to tell us what proposal is being considered? Is it a long runway into the estuary or only a short runway within the dyke? Sixth, will the minister refer the proposals under consideration, whatever they are, back to the airport planning committee if the proposals he is considering are different from those already studied by that committee? Presumably there must be some difference, or the minister would not be talking about further studies or comments. The next point is that if no decision has yet been made-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) I think it is necessary, in order to understand fully what is now taking place with regard to a third runway at Vancouver International Airport, to review some of the recent history of the project.
In 1973 the Ministry of Transport came to the conclusion that a runway parallel to the existing east-west runway was needed at Vancouver International Airport. Terms of reference for an airport planning committee were established, and the first meeting was held in April, 1973. The terms of reference were "to ensure that the proposed development of Vancouver International Airport was compatible with the planning of the various levels of government and the concerns of the public in the communities involved".
Several planning studies were carried out under the supervision of various subcommittees of the airport planning committee. The studies resulted in ten reports, all of which were completed and printed at various times in 1975. During the course of the planning and environmental studies, alternative concepts for a parallel runway were considered, all of which involved extensions past the dyke and into the estuary.
The report of the airport planning committee was printed and made available to the public in March of this year, and the airport planning committee was dissolved. At about this point in time we arrived at the conclusion that instead of implementing one of the concepts involving extension into the estuary we should construct a shorter runway-of approximately 10,000 feet-which could be located entirely within the dyke and which would involve no protrusion into the estuary. We have taken the position that this third runway should not be started before 1978 and that this project is subject to the environmental assessment and review process of the federal government.
[Mr. Fraser.)
November 2, 1976

We have asked that officials of Environment Canada establish an environment assessment panel to review the third runway project. These officials now are considering our request, and we expect a response in the near future.
